articles.title: India-Mexico trade deal: Talks to begin this week amid fresh 50% tariffs on Indian exports | India News - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: India-Mexico trade deal: Talks to begin this week amid fresh 50% tariffs on Indian exports | India News  Hindustan Times
articles.full_text:
India’s merchandise exports to Mexico stood at $5.73 billion in 2025-26, with automobiles accounting for the largest share at $1.92 billion.
India and Mexico will sign the terms of reference (ToR) this week to formally launch negotiations for a preferential trade agreement (PTA), aiming to protect Indian exports from recently imposed high tariffs in the Mexican market, officials said.
The proposed agreement is expected to cover key Indian exports, including automobiles, textiles, footwear, plastics, steel, chemicals and toys, which face tariffs of up to 50% under Mexico’s new tariff regime.
Both countries have finalised the terms of reference and are expected to sign the document in the next couple of days, the officials said, requesting anonymity. Commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal is visiting Mexico from Monday as part of a week-long trade mission that also includes Brussels, the headquarters of the European Union.
The proposed India-Mexico PTA is expected to help Indian exporters mitigate the impact of higher tariffs imposed by the Mexican government on 1,463 items imported from countries that do not have a bilateral trade arrangement with Mexico, such as a PTA or a free trade agreement (FTA).
Experts said signing the terms of reference would mark the first step towards protecting Indian exporters from the higher duties, particularly in the automobile sector.
According to government trade data, India’s merchandise exports to Mexico stood at $5.73 billion in 2025-26, with automobiles accounting for the largest share at $1.92 billion.
The list of products affected by Mexico’s tariff measures includes automobiles, textiles and clothing, plastics, steel, household appliances, aluminium, toys, furniture, footwear, leather goods, paper and cardboard, motorcycles, trailers and glass products.
The tariff measures took effect on January 1 under a decree linked to Mexico’s Plan, which aims to increase domestic content in production chains by 15% by 2030. Launched in January 2025, the initiative seeks to make Mexico one of the world’s 10 largest economies by 2030, revive local industries and create 1.5 million jobs.
PTA seen as faster route to protect exports
Experts said negotiating a bilateral PTA could help India address the tariff challenge more quickly than pursuing a comprehensive FTA, which would take relatively more time to conclude.
One official said the proposed agreement is expected to focus exclusively on preferential trade in goods.
A PTA generally has a limited scope and provides a positive list of products on which tariffs are reduced, though they are rarely eliminated entirely. An FTA, by contrast, seeks to eliminate tariffs on a much wider range of goods, subject to a negative list of excluded items.
India-Mexico trade stood at $7.83 billion in FY26
Bilateral merchandise trade between India and Mexico stood at around $7.83 billion in 2025-26, according to government data.
India exported goods worth approximately $5.73 billion to Mexico during the financial year, while imports from the Latin American country stood at $2.1 billion.
India’s major exports to Mexico include automobiles and auto parts, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and chemical products.
Mexico’s exports to India are dominated by crude oil, which accounts for almost three-fourths of its total shipments to the country. Other products supplied by Mexico include gold and related jewellery, as well as chemical compounds.
The proposed PTA is expected to provide a framework for preferential market access for selected goods, with negotiations set to begin following the formal signing of the terms of reference.

articles.title: India's textile industry targets $350 billion by 2030 as exports rebound, costs rise: Report - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: India's textile industry targets $350 billion by 2030 as exports rebound, costs rise: Report  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The sector reached nearly $190 billion in FY26, with exports rebounding 10.3% in April-August 2026, even as rising cotton yarn prices and US trade uncertainty weigh on manufacturers.
The report noted that the sector remains a primary employment generator while the central government considers a ₹400 billion, five-year Textile Expansion and Employment (TEEM) Scheme to upgrade machinery, deploy advanced technology, and modernise traditional clusters.
The expansion comes as outbound shipments rebound. Textile exports, including handicrafts, grew by 10.3 per cent year-on-year in the April-August 2026 period. The recovery follows a 2.7 per cent decline to $35.8 billion in FY2026, even as imports climbed 17.1 per cent to $9.6 billion.
Tushar Bhaskar, President of Rubix Data Sciences, noted that the sector continues to navigate external headwinds alongside domestic growth.
"India's textile industry has shown resilience, with exports growing 10.3% in April-August 2026 after a 2.7% decline in Dollar terms in FY2026," Bhaskar said.
"At the same time, trade uncertainty in the US market, a rise of approximately 60% in cotton yarn prices, and freight disruptions are adding to the pressure," he added. "This reinforces the importance of diversifying India's export destinations and improving cost competitiveness."
According to the report, the United States remained India's largest destination, taking 31 per cent of shipments in FY2026, followed by the European Union at nearly 16 per cent. However, trade dynamics shifted after the US introduced an additional 10 per cent duty under Section 301 measures in July 2026 concerning forced-labour enforcement, while broader negotiations stalled.
In response, domestic manufacturers accelerated market diversification. Shipments to the US fell approximately 7 per cent in FY2026, while deliveries to major European markets grew 9 per cent. Raymond Lifestyle plans to reduce its US export share from 65 per cent to between 55 and 60 per cent within two years, while Kitex Garments plans to lower its exposure from nearly 100 per cent to between 30 and 35 per cent over the next two to three years.
Input cost inflation also affected the domestic value chain. Cotton yarn prices climbed roughly 60 per cent to ₹400 per kilogram in September 2026 from ₹250 per kilogram in early 2026. The increase coincided with local cotton production dropping to 290.91 lakh bales in the 2025-26 season, down from 352.48 lakh bales in 2020-21. To assist mills, authorities granted an exemption on the 11 per cent cotton import duty through October 31, 2026.
Industrial infrastructure activity provided capital momentum. Investment proposals under the seven approved PM Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel Parks reached ₹685.9 billion by August 2026, led by major expansion outlays from corporate producers including Grasim Industries and Vardhman Textiles.

articles.title: India-EU, UK, EFTA trade pacts to unlock investment, technology partnerships, jobs: Piyush Goyal - India's News.Net
articles.summary: India-EU, UK, EFTA trade pacts to unlock investment, technology partnerships, jobs: Piyush Goyal  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
By Sahil Pandey
The Hague [Netherlands], October 27 (ANI): Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said that the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), along with trade agreements with the UK and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries, will open up significant opportunities for Indian industry, boost investments and create employment on a large scale.
Speaking to ANI in The Hague, Goyal said there was considerable enthusiasm among European countries and Indian businesses over the trade agreements, adding that the pacts would facilitate technological collaboration, strengthen industrial ties and expand opportunities across multiple sectors.
"There is great enthusiasm surrounding the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between the European Union and India. We are leading delegations to various European nations. The Indian industrial sector is seen as holding immense potential. These agreements will pave the way for large-scale investments and extensive technological collaborations," Goyal told ANI.
Highlighting the opportunities in labour-intensive industries, services, education and technology, the minister said the trade agreements would help Indian businesses deepen their presence across European markets.
"Through our agreements with the European Union, including the EFTA nations and the UK, we have effectively opened the entire European market to Indian industry," he said.
Goyal said the agreements would contribute to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of a 'Viksit Bharat 2047', while creating opportunities for farmers, the fishing community, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and educational and technological institutions.
He expressed confidence that the trade pacts would attract substantial investments into India and generate employment opportunities on a large scale.
"I can assure you that there is immense potential between European countries and India. They are as excited as Indian companies. Businesses are looking at complementary strengths and together we believe we will not only be efficient for each other and good for each other, but we will also capture global markets," Goyal said.
The minister's remarks come amid India's efforts to strengthen economic engagement with European partners and expand market access for Indian businesses through trade agreements.
The proposed India-EU FTA is expected to provide a framework for deeper trade and investment ties between the two sides, while India's existing trade agreements with the UK and EFTA countries are aimed at expanding commercial opportunities and strengthening economic cooperation. (ANI)

articles.title: India seeks greater Dutch investment in manufacturing, infrastructure, digital technologies: Piyush Goyal - India's News.Net
articles.summary: India seeks greater Dutch investment in manufacturing, infrastructure, digital technologies: Piyush Goyal  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
The Hague [Netherlands], October 26 (ANI): India and the Netherlands have discussed expanding Dutch investments in India's manufacturing, infrastructure, research and development (R&D) and digital technology sectors, as both countries look to strengthen economic ties and build resilient supply chains.
Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal held discussions with the Netherlands' Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, on Monday, focusing on new opportunities for trade and investment.
Sharing details of the meeting on social media platform X, Goyal said, 'Discussed advancing the India-Netherlands economic partnership through expanded trade, resilient supply chains and greater Dutch investment in India's manufacturing, R&D, infrastructure, renewable energy, logistics and digital technologies.'
The two ministers also explored cooperation in semiconductors, green hydrogen and clean energy, sectors that are important for India's efforts to expand domestic manufacturing and reduce dependence on imports of advanced technologies.
Goyal said they 'explored opportunities for collaboration in semiconductors, green hydrogen and clean energy, while leveraging the India-EU FTA to unlock new avenues for trade and investment.'
In a separate meeting with members of the Dutch Parliament, Goyal discussed opportunities arising from the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), particularly in expanding market access and strengthening supply chains.
He said the discussions covered the agreement's potential to 'boost market access, diversify supply chains, and unlock fresh investment opportunities.'
Goyal also emphasised cooperation in advanced manufacturing, renewable energy and innovation to build a stronger long-term economic partnership.
The discussions come as India and the European Union work towards operationalising their trade agreement, which is expected to provide businesses with greater access to each other's markets.
For India, deeper cooperation with the Netherlands could support investment in technology-intensive manufacturing, clean energy and logistics, while creating opportunities for Indian businesses to expand their presence in European markets.
Goyal also expressed his intention to continue discussions with his Dutch counterpart, saying, 'Look forward to welcoming him to India soon to take these discussions forward.' (ANI)

articles.title: US-Canada tariff deal 'very close', says White House adviser ahead of midterms - The Times of India
articles.summary: US-Canada tariff deal 'very close', says White House adviser ahead of midterms  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
The United States and Canada are moving closer to a trade agreement as tariff negotiations between the two countries gather momentum, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett has said, with the issue carrying political significance ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.
“The negotiations have picked up; they’re gathering steam,” Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, said during an appearance on Fox News’ The Sunday Briefing.
He added that a deal was “very close” and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been speaking with his Canadian counterparts throughout the week.
US President Donald Trump also expressed hope about the negotiations, telling Detroit’s Fox 2 that an agreement could be reached within a couple of months, potentially before the midterm elections.
“We’re getting close to a deal, and a deal could happen that’s going to be very good for everybody,” Trump said.
According to the New York Post, Trump indicated that while an agreement could come before the election, the timeline would depend on whether the terms were favourable to the United States.
“I want to make the right deal,” Trump said, adding that he was focused on the long term rather than securing a quick agreement.
The negotiations come after trade talks between Washington and Ottawa broke down in August, prompting both countries to impose retaliatory measures. The dispute has affected businesses and consumers on both sides of the border and emerged as a political issue in key battleground states ahead of the November 3 elections.
Hassett attributed the earlier difficulties to political developments in Canada, saying the recent Canadian election and tensions involving Alberta had made negotiations particularly difficult.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that he had spoken with Trump about trade and remained willing to negotiate, but stressed that any agreement must serve Canada's interests.
Carney is “ready to sit down and negotiate when the US is”, according to his remarks, while insisting that Ottawa would seek “a deal that’s in the interests of Canadians”.
Canada's minister responsible for US trade negotiations, Dominic LeBlanc, has also been in discussions with Lutnick in recent weeks. A US official told Bloomberg on Sunday that the talks were continuing, although the prospects for an agreement remained uncertain because Washington believed Canada had not yet offered enough.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive negotiations, said Trump would approve only an agreement that benefited the United States.
Trump eases tariffs on some Canadian products
The White House has recently moved to ease tariffs on selected Canadian goods, including following lobbying by Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine.
Collins said on Friday that the administration would remove 50% tariffs on Canadian plywood, bleached paper, cartons and specialised agricultural machinery, with the changes expected to benefit Maine's rural and coastal economies.
Trump had also exempted road salt and other Canadian products from tariffs last month after a request from Collins. At the same time, his administration added duties on certain other goods.
The moves come as Collins faces a competitive re-election contest in Maine, where the economic effects of the trade dispute have become a campaign issue. Her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, criticised the senator for seeking credit for tariff relief, arguing that she had acted because her seat was at risk.
Hassett defended the administration's approach, saying Trump had prioritised Maine's interests.
“President Trump has put the citizens of Maine first,” he said.
The tariff dispute has also become politically significant in Michigan, another battleground state where Republicans face pressure ahead of the midterms. Trump campaigned in the state on Sunday, highlighting the possibility of a trade agreement with Canada.
White House highlights fisheries as priority
Hassett also offered a glimpse into the administration's economic priorities, saying support for fisheries in Maine and Alaska had received particular attention.
“Almost above everything else that we've done at the National Economic Council has been working on Maine and Alaska fisheries,” he said, referring to European regulations that had affected exports of Maine lobster.
Hassett said Trump had negotiated a temporary arrangement with European countries that allowed Maine fishermen to continue shipping their products to Europe.
The administration has also stepped up its focus on the seafood industry. The US Department of Agriculture established its first Office of Seafood in April, while the White House unveiled an “America First Seafood Strategy” on Friday.
The developments highlight how trade policy has become intertwined with domestic political concerns as the administration seeks to support industries and businesses in states crucial to the midterm elections.
For now, however, the US-Canada negotiations remain unresolved. While Trump and Hassett have expressed confidence that an agreement could be within reach, Canadian officials have maintained that any deal must protect the country's economic interests.

About 1,853 ongoing infrastructure projects across 17 central ministries/ departments were monitored, and it was found that the total revised cost was Rs 37,55,803 crore compared to the original cost of Rs 34,33,827 crore.
However, the report did not specify the actual number of projects that faced cost overrun.

The cumulative expenditure on these projects stands at Rs 17.73 lakh crore, accounting for about 47.21 per cent of the project cost, indicating steady progress in implementation.
The Transport & Logistics sector (as per the DEA's Harmonised Master List) accounts for the highest number of ongoing projects (1,320 projects), with a cost of Rs 20.07 lakh crore underscoring priority to connectivity-driven infrastructure growth.
It stated that physical and financial progress broadly move in tandem, with a large number of projects clustered at the initial (0-20 per cent) and advanced (81-100 per cent) stages, indicating a pipeline of newly started projects alongside many nearing completion.
While physical progress exceeds financial progress in the 81-100 per cent range, financial progress is relatively higher in the early stages, reflecting upfront expenditure patterns in project implementation.
The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways accounts for the highest number of projects, with 974 projects (53 per cent out of total projects 1853), and a share of total revised project cost of Rs 9.46 lakh crore (25 per cent of total project cost Rs 37.56 lakh crore), highlighting its central role in national infrastructure development.
The Ministry of Railways has 284 ongoing projects (15 per cent), with a total revised project cost of Rs 7.21 lakh crore (19 per cent).
The Ministry of Coal accounts for 121 ongoing projects (6 per cent), with a total revised project cost of Rs 2.22 lakh crore (6 per cent).
The Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas, Ministry of Power, Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs, and the Department of Water Resources, River Development & GR are implementing 115, 106, 49, and 35 projects, with associated project costs of Rs 4.30 lakh crore, Rs 6.40 lakh crore, Rs 3.41 lakh crore, and Rs 1.95 lakh crore, respectively.
The remaining 169 projects (9 per cent), with a total project cost of Rs 2.62 lakh crore (7 per cent), are distributed across various ministries/departments, including Higher Education, Civil Aviation, Steel, Telecommunications, Labour & Employment, Ports, Shipping & Waterways, Health & Family Welfare, Mines, DPIIT, and Sports.

articles.title: FTA with India will be a game changer in supply chain management: EU ambassador to India - The Economic Times
articles.summary: FTA with India will be a game changer in supply chain management: EU ambassador to India  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: The free trade agreement (FTA) between India and the 
European Union
, expected to be signed in December, and the proposed investment treaty would be a game changer in managing supply chains, according to the EU ambassador to India 
Jean-Eric Paquet
. "I think the negotiation, which concluded at the summit in January, was a game changer, and the 
FTA
 will be a game changer. There is no doubt to be had on that," Paquet told ET.
"The EU Commission proposed signatures a few weeks ago, on the 11th of September. I am mentioning it because with that also comes very detailed information, called a schedule of commitments, where now everyone knows when the taxes, when the rates and import rates are being reduced and entering into force for India," he said. "So, it is a game changer because together with the investment protection agreement-on which negotiations are ongoing, and here I hope we can see an acceleration of these negotiations-when both are in place, it is not just about trade facilitation. It is much more about supply chain management and the resilience of supply chains."
Paquet further said, "We are creating an economic space across India and the European internal market. That is what is being established, creating a long-term perspective and reliability for economic operators, which will obviously build on very significant trade already."
The comments come ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's proposed visit to Brussels in mid-December for the signing of the FTA.
The EU envoy said Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) are very positive about the FTA with India. "A group of MEPs visited India in March, led by the chair of the trade committee in the parliament. They had the opportunity to meet many actors here and get a real sense of the scope of the agreement and how it is being considered so they will be able to deal with it effectively," he said.
Regarding the sensitivities of both sides to the agreement, Paquet said, "We were very careful to ensure that the coverage reflects sensitivities on both sides. It is a free trade agreement which is slightly less broad in agricultural products than others. I think, by and large, both sides were very happy. With the broadest possible coverage of tariff lines-99% of the trade that India has with Europe will be rate-free upon entry into force-we really are covering the sectors that matter, as well as new sectors that have been largely left untouched in the past, such as the automotive sector. Indian car manufacturers are, for the first time, seriously looking at Europe."
Asked about the India-EU Indo-Pacific partnership, the envoy said, "The connection is very strong in terms of supply chains. The Europeans are prioritising their Indo-Pacific strategy, which was adopted a few years ago. We meet on a yearly basis with ministers from the Indo-Pacific region. So, there is really a strong focus on the European side on the Indo-Pacific. India is leading very much on Indo-Pacific foreign policy thinking, and therefore also engaging with us. I think, more concretely, this is about maritime security, freedom of navigation-a big part of the work India and Europe are doing under the security and defence partnership. This is, of course, also about connectivity."
India and the EU are also cooperating on projects in Africa. There could also be scope for Japan, India and Europe to work together, according to the EU envoy.
Referring to the India-EU counterterrorism partnership, he said, "There is a lot of convergence between India and Europe on condemning current terrorism and on root causes of terrorism. I expect this can continue to be very productive."

Nucor Corporation

The United States and Canada are negotiating a deal aimed at easing US tariffs on Canadian steel and automobiles, according to Reuters, as the two governments seek to repair relations that deteriorated after trade talks collapsed in August. The discussions center on duties imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on autos, with negotiators exploring possible relief from those measures.
The talks are taking place as US President Donald Trump contends with record-low approval ratings and as his Republican Party faces the risk of losing control of Congress in midterm elections in the coming weeks. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a political liability for the President, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade dispute with Canada.
A Canadian source briefed on the negotiations indicated that a deal on steel and auto tariffs could be reached before the November 3 elections, while US sources said the administration wants Canada to make additional concessions. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because the talks are private.
Because the Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is at the center of the negotiations rather than the US Trade Representative's office, according to sources on both sides of the border. Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc, the Canadian minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently, one source said.
A spokesperson for LeBlanc said Canada remains in constructive dialogue with its US counterparts on a range of priorities and stands ready to work in good faith toward a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canadian interests. A US Trade Representative official said that office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days regarding the overall architecture of any deal and other trade issues. The White House and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there had been a slight intensification in talks with the United States and that Ottawa had not changed its stance. He told reporters that any progress reflected the US moving closer to Canada's position, without providing details.
A Canadian industry source said a deal could come quickly but might not be broad, suggesting that if an agreement happens it would likely be narrowed in scope.

articles.title: Piyush Goyal meets North Holland’s King’s Commissioner in The Hague, placing regional investment and India-EU trade links in focus - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Piyush Goyal meets North Holland’s King’s Commissioner in The Hague, placing regional investment and India-EU trade links in focus  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal held a meeting with Arthur van Dijk, King’s Commissioner of the Province of North Holland, in The Hague on Monday, October 26. The 30-minute engagement, listed by the North Holland provincial government, was also attended by Indian Ambassador Kumar Tuhin and formed part of Goyal’s wider Netherlands visit to expand trade, investment and industrial cooperation.
The meeting comes as Goyal leads a delegation of about 100 Indian businesses and startups to Germany and the Netherlands from October 22 to 27. India’s Commerce Ministry has said the Europe tour is intended to deepen economic partnerships, expand bilateral trade and advance cooperation in manufacturing, technology, clean energy, logistics and resilient supply chains.
Why North Holland matters
North Holland is home to Amsterdam and parts of the Netherlands’ high-value logistics, technology and innovation ecosystem. A meeting with the province’s King’s Commissioner gives India’s trade outreach a sub-national dimension, connecting national-level trade policy with regional investment authorities and business networks.
The Netherlands is also a key European gateway for Indian goods and investment. Goyal visited the Port of Rotterdam on October 25, where he met port chief executive Boudewijn Siemons; the government described Rotterdam as Europe’s largest port and an important entry point for Indian exports into European markets.India-EU trade context
The Hague leg includes meetings with the Dutch Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate and the Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. The stated agenda covers expanded trade channels and cooperation on green-transition initiatives, alongside engagement with Dutch parliamentary committees on foreign trade and European affairs.
The visit takes place against the backdrop of negotiations for a proposed India-European Union free trade agreement. Indian officials have projected the Netherlands’ ports, logistics infrastructure and European connectivity as potentially important channels for Indian exporters if tariff and market-access barriers are reduced.
Business forum follows
Later on Monday, Goyal is scheduled to address the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague alongside the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation. The forum will be followed by six parallel sectoral roundtables and business-to-business networking sessions.
The roundtables will cover agri-food and food processing, high technology and innovation, sustainability and renewable energy, logistics and supply-chain connectivity, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, textiles, engineering goods and services. No agreement, investment announcement or joint statement from the Goyal–van Dijk meeting had been issued at the time of reporting.
Why it matters
The meeting signals India’s effort to build economic ties beyond national capitals by engaging provincial governments that control or influence regional investment promotion, infrastructure and innovation networks. For Indian firms, such contacts can help identify opportunities in Dutch ports, clean technology, advanced manufacturing and logistics services.
For the Netherlands, deeper engagement with India offers access to one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies and a large market for Dutch expertise in water management, ports, agri-food technology and renewable energy.
What comes next
Attention will now shift to the India-Netherlands Business Forum and sectoral roundtables in The Hague. Any follow-up announcements on investments, MoUs, trade-facilitation measures or India-EU FTA-related cooperation will help show whether Monday’s meetings produced concrete outcomes.

articles.title: 'Very High' Expectations From India-EU Trade Deal, Says Rotterdam Port Chief - Siliconindia
articles.summary: 'Very High' Expectations From India-EU Trade Deal, Says Rotterdam Port Chief  Siliconindia
articles.full_text:
The Rotterdam port chief says expectations from the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) are very high, highlighting the potential to expand bilateral trade and strengthen logistics links. The proposed deal could create new opportunities for exporters, improve market access, and deepen supply chain cooperation between India and Europe.
	Boudewijn Siemons, Chief Executive Officer of the Port of Rotterdam, expects the proposed India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to significantly expand commercial ties between the two economies, as businesses prepare for greater trade flows, improved market access and stronger supply chain connectivity. Siemons said Europe sees substantial opportunities in India's expanding economy and expects bilateral business activity to increase as the trade agreement advances.
"I have very high expectations from the FTA, and I think with the developments in India going on, the potential is huge. And I think Europe is really looking forward to doing more and more business with India", Siemons told reporters at the port.
His remarks follow India's announcement with the 27-member European Union in January that negotiations for the trade pact have concluded. The agreement is expected to be signed by the end of 2026 and could come into effect in 2027, subject to the required approval and implementation procedures. The proposed deal aims to strengthen economic engagement by improving access to each other's markets and creating new opportunities for exporters, manufacturers and service providers.
Siemons made the comments during a visit by India's Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal to the Port of Rotterdam on Sunday. Their discussions covered the importance of closer cooperation between ports and countries in a global economy where international trade depends on reliable logistics networks, efficient cargo handling and coordinated supply chain operations.
	Also Read: India Seeks Advanced Manufacturing, Semiconductor and Defense Imports Ahead of EU Trade Deal
"making sure that the goods can flow more easily between India and Europe is something that we will be working on", Siemons told reporters.
The Port of Rotterdam holds a strategic position in European trade, serving as a major gateway for cargo entering and leaving the continent. Stronger links with Indian ports and businesses could help improve the movement of goods, strengthen maritime connectivity and create opportunities across shipping, warehousing, freight forwarding and other logistics services.
For Indian exporters, improved trade access and more efficient cargo movement could support greater competitiveness in European markets. Manufacturers of engineering goods, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, textiles, machinery and other export-oriented products could benefit from stronger commercial connections, although the actual impact will depend on the agreement's final provisions, tariff changes and implementation.
European businesses could also find opportunities in India's growing demand for advanced manufacturing equipment, industrial technologies, energy solutions and infrastructure development. Better market access could encourage companies to expand distribution networks, establish partnerships and evaluate fresh investment opportunities in India.
However, the commercial gains will depend on more than tariff reductions. Port infrastructure, customs procedures, documentation requirements, shipping schedules and coordination between logistics operators will influence how effectively businesses use the agreement. Closer cooperation between Indian and European ports could help address these operational challenges and improve supply chain predictability.
The proposed FTA therefore represents an opportunity to strengthen both trade policy and physical connectivity. As India and Europe move toward the agreement's signing, cooperation between major logistics gateways such as Rotterdam and Indian ports could become increasingly important in translating improved market access into sustained growth in bilateral trade and investment.

articles.title: Has Pakistan reopened its border with Iran for trade? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Has Pakistan reopened its border with Iran for trade?  Al JazeeraPakistan reopens Gabd-Rimdan border crossing with Iran  The HinduThousands of trucks stuck as partial Iran-Pakistan trade resumes  Arab NewsIran-Pakistan border trade serves mutual interests: ambassador  Tehran TimesIntense clashes reported near the Iran-Pakistan border  Latest news from Azerbaijan
articles.full_text:
Islamabad, Pakistan – On a normal day, hundreds of freight trucks and vehicles pass through Pakistan-Iran border crossings, carrying goods and people. On October 17, Islamabad suspended cargo traffic through the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings in Balochistan province, citing security risks.
On Monday, some goods started to move again.
Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Al Jazeera that trade “partially resumed this weekend”.
Border officials also cleared consignments that were dated from October 16 or earlier, goods truck association officials said.
Haji Noor Muhammad Shahwani, central president of the Balochistan Goods Truck Owners Association, told Al Jazeera from Quetta that Pakistani exports such as rice and bananas were crossing the border.
Trucks loaded in Iran before the closure, including those carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), were also entering Pakistan, he confirmed to Al Jazeera. “Those that were already loaded are clearing and coming out now. They are coming slowly.”
The halt of Iranian LPG to Pakistan created severe shortages and price spikes in Pakistan, which imports the bulk of its energy from the Middle East. Pakistan’s economy has already been impacted by shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by Iran and its response to the United States-Israel war.
Rizwan Ahmed, a customs clearing agent based near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing said customs had told agents to file declarations for the stranded trucks, which would then be released.
“Customs has given us the go-ahead, saying, ‘Bring in as much cargo as you can,’” Ahmed told Al Jazeera. He did not say whether this applied to goods loaded after October 16.
Ahmed said his own consignment of exports had just left. “We have rice, retail goods, potatoes, bananas,” he told Al Jazeera.
Cargo held up at the crossing
But Iran said changes to import paperwork introduced by Islamabad are holding up its cargo at the crossings.
On Sunday, Iran’s ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said on X that Iran had placed no restrictions on exports to Pakistan, including LPG, and its borders remained open.
“Changes in the implementation of Pakistan’s E-Form procedure for imports from Iran have created a situation in which traders are effectively and literally unable to dispatch cargo from Iran to Pakistan,” he wrote.
The halt in trade between the two neighbours triggered speculation that the Pakistani step might have been taken under US pressure as part of Washington’s efforts to suffocate Iran economically. Pakistan insisted it was done amid a deteriorating security situation in Balochistan province on the border with Iran.
Gunmen attacked trucks waiting near the Gabd crossing on the Pakistani side of the border on Thursday. The military said 10 attackers were killed in operations around Gabd and Gwadar city, and one civilian died.
The attack came in a province that has faced a separatist rebellion for decades.
Balochistan accounted for 131 of the 225 armed attacks recorded nationwide in September, the highest monthly national total in 12 years, according to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs was asked about the border at its weekly news briefing on Friday.
“Pakistan, as a responsible member of the international community, adheres to and shall continue to adhere to all applicable sanctions regimes in accordance with international and domestic laws,” spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said.
He said he did not have direct knowledge of the situation on the ground. He did not say whether the border was open or whether the US had pressured Pakistan over the closure.
The Ministry of Commerce did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The paperwork dispute
A Commerce Ministry memorandum from October 16, seen by Al Jazeera, withdrew its October 3 memorandum extending a waiver on the E-Form, also called the EIF, for imports from Iran. It took effect immediately.
The purpose of the E-Form is to record imports and their payment through banks.
Moghadam, the Iranian envoy, said consultations with Pakistan were under way. Citing reports, he added that several hundred LPG trucks had crossed into Gabd but were yet to be unloaded or cleared.
Shahwani, from the Balochistan Goods Truck Owners Association, said the unloading problem had not been resolved.
“It is probably some problem with the banks, something to do with international trade,” he said.
Bakhtiar Ismail, the deputy commissioner of Chagai in Balochistan, wrote on X on October 18 that the closure was a temporary measure to improve border management and support counterterrorism efforts.
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei cited technical issues, according to the IRNA news agency.
Sanctions in the background
Pakistan has mediated between Washington and Tehran since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28. The US has since imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports, impacting Iranian exports. The US has also imposed wide-ranging economic sanctions to “asphyxiate” the Iranian government and cut off its revenue streams.
Imtiaz Baloch, a security analyst who focuses on Balochistan, told Al Jazeera that the US policy of maximum pressure on Iran had a direct or indirect influence.
That could be done directly, by forcing Pakistan’s government to close the border, or indirectly, through companies in the LPG trade or international banking channels, he said. But he added that no concrete or visible statement had linked the closure to US economic policy.
“My assessment is that security is part of it, procedures or technical glitches are part of it and the banking system is also involved,” Baloch said.

articles.title: US-EU aircraft trade truce under strain - The Hans India
articles.summary: US-EU aircraft trade truce under strain  The Hans India
articles.full_text:
Washington:  The United States has warned that a record-breaking European investment loan to aircraft manufacturer Airbus has injected fresh uncertainty into transatlantic trade, raising questions about the future of an agreement under which Washington and Brussels suspended punitive tariffs in their long-running aircraft subsidy dispute.   
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Monday expressed concern over the European Investment Bank's decision to extend what he described as its largest-ever loan to Airbus, saying Washington had yet to receive details of the financing despite repeated requests.  
The loan, intended to benefit Airbus projects in France, Germany and Spain, has revived a dispute over government support for aircraft manufacturers that the United States and European Union had sought to contain through an agreement suspending retaliatory duties.  
“I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past,” Greer said in a statement issued by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).  
The American trade official accused France, Germany and Spain of providing longstanding support to Airbus that disadvantaged US aerospace companies and workers.  
“For decades, France, Germany, and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and businesses,” he said.  
Greer's intervention places renewed attention on the terms of the transatlantic aircraft agreement, particularly provisions requiring financing for large civil aircraft manufacturers to be provided on commercial terms.  
The United States has not announced new tariffs or formally declared that the European Union violated the agreement. However, Greer's remarks signal that Washington is questioning whether the financing arrangement is consistent with the commitments made by both sides.  
According to the USTR, the European Investment Bank approved the loan during the summer, shortly after the European Union extended the suspension of duties associated with the aircraft dispute.  
The US trade representative said the timing of the decision and the lack of information about the loan had raised concerns in Washington.  
“Despite ongoing requests, USTR still has no details about this loan,” Greer said.  
He added that the development had created substantial uncertainty for transatlantic aerospace trade and called for the matter to be resolved quickly.  
“It is important this situation is resolved as soon as possible to ensure market-driven production in the aerospace sector and to avoid violation of the terms of our hard-won LCA deal,” he said.  
The latest disagreement comes against the backdrop of one of the longest-running trade disputes between the United States and Europe, involving competing allegations of government subsidies to Boeing and Airbus.  
The World Trade Organization authorised retaliatory measures in the aircraft disputes after findings concerning support provided to both manufacturers. Washington and Brussels subsequently agreed in 2021 to suspend related tariffs for five years while pursuing a negotiated framework for large civil aircraft financing.  
The arrangement was intended to reduce trade friction between the two economies while establishing principles governing government support for aircraft production. The renewed US concerns highlight the importance of those financing commitments to the durability of the agreement.

The Hague [Netherlands], October 27 (ANI): India and the US have concluded most discussions on the proposed bilateral trade agreement and are now fine-tuning the pact, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday, signalling progress in negotiations amid continuing tariff-related uncertainties.

Washington, Oct 27 (IANS) The White House said that the Trump administration was engaged in “productive talks” with India on a “historic trade deal”, hours after Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the two sides had concluded most of the discussions and were fine-tuning the agreement.
“Representatives of the Trump administration continue to engage in productive talks with Indian officials to secure a historic trade deal that puts Americans and America First,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told IANS.
“President Trump and Prime Minister Modi have a close personal relationship, and both leaders remain committed to lifting bilateral ties to new levels,” Middleton said.
Speaking at the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague on Monday, Goyal said: “We have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement.”
Goyal is in the Netherlands as part of a visit to Germany and the Netherlands with a business delegation. He also said India had concluded nine free trade agreements in the last four and a half years.
India and the US announced the framework for the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement in February. Under the framework announced on February 7, the US cut the tariff on Indian goods to 18 per cent from 50 per cent. Subsequent changes in US tariff policy, including after the US Supreme Court ruling on tariffs, led to further negotiations.
Goyal met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministerial in Milwaukee on October 1. A team led by Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal held talks with US officials in Washington from October 15 to 17.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during his visit to Mumbai on October 20, said the two sides were close to an agreement.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without (inaudible) agreement. I think there’s a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” Rubio told reporters.
“Obviously the State Department doesn’t negotiate trade agreements, but we are very much involved in what’s happening,” Rubio said.
The trade negotiations have been closely watched in both countries, with Washington pressing New Delhi to buy more American energy and technology, and Indian exporters seeking relief from US tariffs.
India has said it intends to buy $500 billion worth of US energy products, aircraft and aircraft parts, precious metals, technology products and coking coal over five years.

articles.title: Beyond recovery: Policy priorities to achieve durable growth in Sri Lanka - Island.lk
articles.summary: Beyond recovery: Policy priorities to achieve durable growth in Sri Lanka  Island.lk
articles.full_text:
By Rashmi Anupama and Kalani Kiriveldeniya, Research Assistants, Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS)
Sustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties.
IPS Research Fellows Dr Asanka Wijesinghe and Dr Lakmini Fernando presented key findings, followed by interventions from Dr Yashodha Senadheera, Deputy Director of the Economic Research Department of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL); Dr Liliya Aleksanyan, Senior Country Economist for Sri Lanka at the Asian Development Bank (ADB); Sanjaya Ariyawansa, Senior Economist at Sampath Bank; and other invited parties.
Growth Has Returned, but Can Sri Lanka Sustain It?
Dr Asanka Wijesinghe discussed Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic performance, external sector competitiveness, and policy priorities for durable growth. He highlighted that while the economy’s recovery has been satisfactory, sustained annual growth of approximately 8.3% between 2026 and 2030 would be required to regain the pre-crisis growth trajectory. Against this background, Sri Lanka needs to accelerate reforms towards achieving stated medium-term growth target of 7% or above.
Rising global fuel prices and the resulting external sector pressures pose an immediate challenge to Sri Lanka’s economic growth. Sri Lanka recorded a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 4.2% in the second quarter of 2026, with increased contribution of investment to economic output. However, the increased import bill has been a drag on output growth. The merchandise trade deficit widened considerably during January–August 2026, when compared to 2025.
Improvements in fiscal consolidation and debt management have given Sri Lanka breathing space amidst a hostile external sector. Dr Wijesinghe stressed the need to maintain fiscal discipline, strengthen external competitiveness, and continue engagement with international financial institutions as the country rebuilds its resilience.
Strengthening Export Competitiveness
Dr Wijesinghe emphasised that expansion of exports is essential for achieving 7% economic growth, as growth driven primarily by domestic demand has its limitations.
Sri Lanka’s reliance on non-reciprocal preferential market access faces growing challenges as competing economies negotiate reciprocal trade agreements. For example, Indonesia’s preferential access to the European Union (EU) and India’s trade agreement with the United Kingdom (UK) could weaken Sri Lanka’s competitiveness. This challenge could be further compounded by the potential loss of existing preferential arrangements for Sri Lanka, including the Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+).
Securing more predictable tariff regimes in major export markets is a necessary precondition, and it requires accelerating tariff reforms and simplifying the tariff structure. However, these reforms must be carefully sequenced, as sudden reductions in tariff protection could adversely affect domestic industries, particularly Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). He also recommended a dedicated fund to support trade adjustment.
Reorienting Fiscal Policy Towards Long-Term Growth
Building on these discussions, Dr Lakmini Fernando explained how fiscal policy could support durable growth beyond the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme. During the adjustment period, government capital expenditure declined to historically low levels, constraining the scope for public investment to support long-term growth and development.
Achieving 7% economic growth could require gross fixed capital formation equivalent to approximately 30–42% of GDP, depending on investment efficiency. Mobilising such investment also requires a supportive environment for private investment alongside productive public expenditure.
She also highlighted the need to prioritise education, healthcare, skills development, social protection, climate-resilient infrastructure, and green investment to meet evolving future demand. Improving public financial management, strengthening project implementation capacity, and ensuring transparent and competitive procurement were also identified as essential reforms.
On debt sustainability, Dr Fernando stressed adhering to a medium-term debt management strategy, strengthening fiscal institutions, and exploring innovative financing. Continued engagement with international financial institutions could ease financing pressures. She also highlighted the importance of long-term planning and consistent implementation.
Expert Perspectives: Monetary Stability, Economic Resilience, and Emerging Shocks
Dr Yashodha Senadheera elaborated on the Central Bank’s monetary policy response to external supply-side shocks. She explained that although monetary policy has limited capacity to directly address supply-driven inflation, intervention may become necessary when such shocks generate persistent inflationary pressures or threaten inflation expectations. Maintaining price stability while considering broader economic conditions therefore requires careful, data-driven policy decisions.
Dr Liliya Aleksanyan highlighted the lasting effects of successive crises and global energy-price volatility, emphasising the need for greater energy security through renewable energy. She also encouraged Sri Lanka to explore Asian export markets like India, alongside traditional markets such as EU and the United States of America (USA). Additionally, she highlighted the importance of preparing for emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence
Sanjaya Ariyawansa focused on revenue mobilisation and climate risks. He called for improvements in tax administration, integration of SMEs into the tax system, and independent fiscal oversight. He also urged closer assessment of how climate-related shocks could affect agriculture, energy, public expenditure, and banking sector stability to strengthen preparedness and resilience.
From Policy Recommendations to Implementation
The subsequent roundtable discussion further explored several themes raised during the presentations and expert interventions. Participants discussed the assumptions underlying growth projections, the investment required to achieve higher growth, and opportunities to strengthen revenue mobilisation. To overcome the persistent gap between budgetary allocations and actual expenditure, participants also focused on improving the efficiency and timely utilisation of public investment.
The discussion also explored fiscal responses to energy price shocks, the importance of supporting industries affected by tariff reforms, and the potential contribution of innovative climate financing instruments. Participants underscored that strengthening institutional capacity and anticipating risks are equally important as designing appropriate policies.
The Way Forward
The growth trajectory demands complementary reforms across macroeconomic management, international trade, public investment, fiscal institutions, and climate resilience. Ultimately, Sri Lanka’s long-term economic prospects will depend both on identifying the right policy priorities and implementing them consistently. As emphasised throughout the discussion, durable growth requires a forward-looking development strategy that strengthens the country’s capacity to withstand future shocks while delivering sustained improvements in economic well-being.

articles.title: Iran says Mecca pact states agree to boost cooperation - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Iran says Mecca pact states agree to boost cooperation  Al JazeeraMecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions  Al JazeeraSaudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks  ReutersPakistan, Saudi, Turkey Meet Iran leaders In Bid To Stop War Restarting  NDTVAsim Munir returns to Tehran as Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye seek to contain regional crisis  Telegraph India
articles.full_text:
Iran has said it will continue discussions with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye amid escalating tensions that have threatened regional stability and shaken the global economy.
The announcement came as top Iranian military officials met with senior Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials on Monday in what Iranian state television described as their first joint meeting.
Pakistan and Turkiye are strong allies of Saudi Arabia and have pledged military support to Riyadh as part of their new mutual defence pact, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The meeting in Tehran was held after Saudi Arabia faced weeks of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are fighting forces with the country’s internationally recognised and Saudi-backed government.
The meeting, which focused on “peace and security in the region”, was hosted by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
A statement issued by Iranian officials after the meeting said participants “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation between the four regional countries”, according to Iran’s Fars news agency.
Saudi Arabia and its allies have not commented on the meeting or reported agreement.
Rayed Krimly, the Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy, said earlier today that the visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement allies “for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis and promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions in support of the mediation efforts carried out” by Qatar and Pakistan.
“The visit underscores the pivotal role of Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries in reinforcing regional security and stability and working with all countries in the region to achieve that goal,” he wrote on X.
Turkiye’s state news agency Anadolu reported that Kalin will attend the meeting in Tehran, citing Turkish security sources.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and the three members of the alliance since Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi armed group escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia last month.
Pakistan’s Field Marshal Munir last week visited Tehran, where he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials.
During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with the United States about ending the US-Israel war on Iran until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan has been a key intermediary between Washington and Tehran since the US and Israel launched the war in February.
Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the US resumed weeks later.
Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued.
Ministers from the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli war on Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August. Under it, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and internationally recognised borders, according to the text publicised at the time.
Efforts by Turkiye’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

articles.title: India, US fine-tuning trade deal after concluding most discussions, says minister Piyush Goyal - Livemint
articles.summary: India, US fine-tuning trade deal after concluding most discussions, says minister Piyush Goyal  Livemint
articles.full_text:
THE HAGUE: India and the US have concluded most discussions on a proposed trade agreement and are fine-tuning the deal, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday, signalling progress towards an agreement that could bring greater certainty to Indian exporters facing shifting US tariff policies.
“In the last four and a half years, friends, we have entered into nine free trade agreements or bilateral trade agreements. I'm adding the US in that, we have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement,” Goyal said at the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague.
For Indian exporters, a deal could provide greater predictability in pricing US-bound shipments and negotiating contracts. Any boost to exports would also offer timely support to an economy grappling with the fallout from the wars in West Asia and Ukraine.
Goyal’s remarks follow a recent visit to India by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the two countries were “very, very close” to a trade agreement, with a small number of issues remaining to be resolved.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without (inaudible) agreement. I think there’s a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” Rubio had said.
Goyal said India’s expanding network of trade agreements, including those under negotiation, would give it preferential access to economies accounting for $85 trillion of the $115 trillion global GDP.
“Just to give you the context of India thinking on opening our doors. Until 2014, all the free trade agreements put together opened a GDP of $10 trillion where we had preferential access or where we opened our doors to those countries,” said Goyal, who is on an official visit to the Netherlands.
“India would have opened its doors and had preferential market access to an additional $60 trillion worth of economies around the globe. Together, now we have $70 trillion of economies where we would have preferential trade agreements. I have eight more negotiations which are underway right now which will add another $15 trillion. So India would be opening its doors to $85 trillion out of $115 trillion. That's around 76% of global GDP with which we are building our partnership, opening the doors on a complementary and cooperative nature to greater business engagement,” Goyal said.
Bilateral trade between India and the US rose 6.53% to $140.76 billion in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), from $132.2 billion in the previous year. India’s trade surplus narrowed to $33.9 billion from $40.9 billion. Exports to the US edged up to $87.31 billion from $86.51 billion, while imports rose 17.16% to $53.45 billion from $45.62 billion.
The proposed agreement comes as global supply chains face disruption from the wars in West Asia and Ukraine, alongside a broader global slowdown. Goods exports remain important to India’s growth, with provisional commerce ministry data showing merchandise exports rose 23% year-on-year to $44.4 billion in September. Imports increased 8% to $74.61 billion, narrowing the trade deficit to $30.21 billion from $33 billion a year earlier.
Goyal said India remained on track for strong growth despite international uncertainties.
“Despite all the problems of the world, we are the fastest growing large economy. We grew 7.7% last year. The IMF (International Monetary Fund) just came out with numbers…We're expected to go upward of 7%. My own guess is we'll grow 7.5% this year,” he said.
The IMF has raised its growth forecast for India by 60 basis points to 7% for FY27, reinforcing its position as the fastest-growing major economy.
Ramita Mishra contributed to the story.
The writer is in The Hague as the guest of Confederation of Indian Industry.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW: India–US Trade Tensions, Russian Oil and Maritime Security: Adv. Vatsal Verghese on the Geopolitics Shaping Global Commerce - Business Upturn
articles.summary: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW: India–US Trade Tensions, Russian Oil and Maritime Security: Adv. Vatsal Verghese on the Geopolitics Shaping Global Commerce  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
The India–United States relationship is entering a consequential phase, as the two countries attempt to consolidate their economic partnership amid shifting tariff policies, energy security concerns and competing geopolitical priorities. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's October visit to India, his second in less than five months, has brought these tensions into sharper focus, with trade negotiations, energy cooperation and strategic engagement dominating the bilateral agenda.
The proposed trade agreement has emerged as a central issue in the relationship.
The tariff dispute has demonstrated how trade policy can become an instrument of foreign policy. Washington's pressure over India's Russian crude purchases, combined with the threat of additional duties, has created uncertainty for exporters, refiners, shipping companies and international traders. On October 16, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order waiving key provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which had authorised substantial duties and sanctions. The move provided immediate relief, but it did not eliminate the underlying policy uncertainty.
Energy cooperation offers another dimension to the relationship. India's substantial refining capacity, its position in global petroleum trade and its commercial links with diverse suppliers have made it an important participant in discussions surrounding energy diversification. At the same time, maritime routes, freight economics, sanctions compliance and the security of critical chokepoints remain essential considerations for businesses operating across international markets.
To examine the legal, commercial and strategic implications of these developments, we speak with Adv. Vatsal Verghese, a maritime law, international trade and geopolitics professional with approximately 25 years of experience.
Q1. The India–US relationship is being described as strategically important, yet trade disagreements continue to complicate it. How should we understand this apparent contradiction?
Adv. Vatsal Verghese: I would distinguish between strategic convergence and commercial alignment. The two countries can share substantial interests in maritime security, technology, defence cooperation and the stability of the Indo-Pacific without necessarily agreeing on tariffs, market access or domestic economic priorities.
A strategic partnership is not a guarantee of frictionless trade. In fact, as bilateral commerce expands, disagreements become more consequential because the number of affected industries, investments and contractual relationships increases.
For businesses, the important question is not whether the political relationship is described as positive. It is whether the underlying commercial environment is sufficiently predictable to support investment decisions over five, ten or twenty years.
That is where trade agreements, regulatory clarity and dispute-resolution mechanisms become essential. Political engagement creates opportunities, but durable commercial confidence requires enforceable rules, transparent procedures and consistency in implementation.
Q2. On October 26, India indicated that the trade negotiations had entered a fine-tuning stage. What does this mean commercially, and should businesses interpret it as a near-certain agreement?
Adv. Vatsal Verghese: Progress in negotiations is encouraging, but I would caution against equating political optimism with legal completion.
A trade agreement is not concluded simply because the parties have resolved most of their disagreements. The remaining provisions can determine the commercial value of the entire arrangement. Rules of origin, tariff schedules, product-specific exclusions, safeguards, customs procedures and the treatment of sensitive sectors can have substantial consequences.
There is also a distinction between reaching political agreement, completing legal drafting, signing the instrument and bringing it into force. Each stage has its own requirements.
Businesses should therefore prepare for possible implementation scenarios rather than make irreversible commitments based on expectations of a signature.
For exporters, I would recommend reviewing their product classifications, origin documentation, supplier contracts and pricing models. The prudent approach is to identify what becomes commercially viable under different tariff outcomes.
An agreement may create significant opportunities, but the final text, not the announcement, will determine the rights and obligations of businesses.
Q3. The United States has used tariffs in connection with its broader foreign policy, including pressure over Russian oil purchases. Does this fundamentally alter the traditional understanding of international trade law?
Adv. Vatsal Verghese: It reinforces something that international trade practitioners have understood for years: trade law does not operate independently of national security and foreign policy.
Tariffs are ordinarily associated with trade protection, industrial policy or negotiated market access. But when governments connect duties to another country's energy procurement or geopolitical conduct, the economic instrument acquires a strategic function.
From a legal perspective, one must examine the precise statutory authority, the applicable international obligations, the scope of exemptions and the mechanisms available for review or challenge. It would be incorrect to assume that every tariff measure is automatically unlawful, or that invoking national security automatically settles its legality.
For India, the challenge is to protect commercial interests while preserving its ability to make sovereign decisions concerning energy security.
For businesses, the lesson is that geopolitical conduct can become a cost variable. Procurement, financing, shipping and customer contracts must increasingly account for policy risks originating outside the immediate commercial transaction.
Q4. The October 16 US executive order waived key provisions of the Graham Act. How much relief does this provide to Indian businesses, and what risks remain?
Adv. Vatsal Verghese: The waiver provides meaningful near-term relief by reducing the immediate threat of additional duties and sanctions under the provisions covered by the order. It also reduces the risk of an abrupt disruption to energy procurement and associated trade flows.
However, relief and certainty are not the same thing.
The order relies on statutory waiver authority and includes a framework for monitoring developments and considering further action. It also does not erase every pre-existing sanctions restriction or every compliance obligation that may apply to a transaction.
An Indian company should not interpret a waiver as a blanket clearance for all Russian-origin cargoes, vessels, counterparties or financial arrangements.
Compliance must be assessed transaction by transaction. The parties must identify the actual supplier, beneficial ownership, vessel interests, insurers, banks, cargo origin and any applicable restrictions.
The commercial risk is particularly significant when a company commits to a long-term contract but the regulatory position is capable of changing during its performance.
My recommendation would be to incorporate appropriate sanctions-change provisions, alternative sourcing mechanisms, suspension rights and clearly allocated costs into contracts, while ensuring that these provisions do not purport to authorise conduct prohibited by applicable law.
Q5. India continues to balance affordable Russian crude with energy diversification. How should the country approach this issue without compromising either energy security or its international trade relationships?
Adv. Vatsal Verghese: Energy security must be evaluated through the combined lens of affordability, availability, reliability and geopolitical exposure.
A crude procurement decision cannot be made exclusively on the basis of the headline price. A discounted cargo may become substantially less attractive after accounting for freight, insurance, financing, refinery compatibility, payment restrictions and the probability of delay.
India's refining sector has considerable commercial capabilities, but its purchasing decisions remain exposed to global supply conditions and external regulatory developments.
Diversification should therefore be treated as a portfolio strategy. This means maintaining access to multiple suppliers, grades, shipping arrangements and delivery routes rather than replacing one dependency with another.
The United States can be an important supplier, but so can other commercially viable sources. The objective should not be to politicise every procurement decision. It should be to maximise energy security while complying with applicable law.
A resilient energy policy is one in which the country retains alternatives when prices, regulations or maritime conditions change.
Q6. The Jamnagar refinery has become an important part of discussions on US–India energy cooperation, particularly regarding heavy crude. What makes refining capacity a geopolitical asset?
Adv. Vatsal Verghese: Refining capacity gives a country a different position in the energy value chain.
Producing crude is one form of energy power. Having the infrastructure, technology and commercial capability to process diverse crude grades is another.
As highlighted in the recent bilateral discussions, India has facilities capable of processing certain heavy crude grades, including Venezuelan crude. But compatibility must be assessed refinery by refinery, based on configuration, crude assays, operating economics and product demand.
The strategic advantage lies in the ability to purchase from a broader range of suppliers and convert those inputs into commercially valuable refined products.
