articles.title: India's Job Crisis: The Disconnect Between Economic Growth, Education And Employment - ETV Bharat
articles.summary: India's Job Crisis: The Disconnect Between Economic Growth, Education And Employment  ETV Bharat
articles.full_text:
India has been facing a unique situation in which robust economic growth does not automatically translate into increased job opportunities, writes M. Venkateshwarlu
India's GDP growth has been robust, supported by political stability and sustained capital formation. But this impressive performance has not translated equally into employment generation, as the unemployment rate is rising. This disconnect between strong GDP growth, rising investment, and increasing unemployment needs closer examination.
Historically, the data reveal that unemployment has evolved from predominantly rural and seasonal to more complex forms, reflecting changes in the structure of the Indian economy, employment patterns, technology, education and skill requirements. Thus, the unemployment problem is much more complex than what the data suggest.
The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) surveys reveal that India's unemployment rate was moderate, at around 2-3%, during the 1990s and 2000s. The unemployment rate increased to 2.3% in 2011-2012 and rose sharply to 6% in 2017-18, as per the new Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) Framework. In the following years, unemployment declined to 5.8% in 2018-19 and continued to decline, reaching 3.1% in 2025.
On the other hand, the average unemployment rate among qualified youth aged 15 to 29 years was 9.9% in 2025, a 0.4 percentage point decrease from 10.3% in 2024. The unemployment rate in urban areas was 13.6%, compared to 8.3% in rural areas for the same period.
However, the most critical issue is the persistently high rate of graduate unemployment, which is alarming. The official PLFS data reveal that unemployment among graduates aged 15 and above was 17.2% in 2019-20 and declined to around 13% in 2023-24. Therefore, the unemployment problem is more pronounced among qualified youth, with rates significantly above the overall average.
The International Labour Organisation (ILO) estimated that around 29.1% of young graduates were unemployed in 2022. The unemployment rate among women graduates was 34.5%, compared with 26.4% among young men.
Interpretation of the above-stated unemployment figures is difficult and may not be accurate. In a true sense, the reported unemployment rates do not capture underemployment or the real problem of highly qualified individuals working in low-paying jobs that do not match their skills and qualifications. As stated in the ILO-IHD India Employment Report 2024, highly educated young people accounted for more than half of unemployed non-student youth in 2022.
A large young population represents a valuable demographic dividend, as it is viewed as a potential productive workforce. However, to realise its benefits, young people must have access to quality, skills-based education and vocational training that align with the changing requirements of the labour market. Therefore, converting the demographic dividend into sustained economic growth requires a combination of human capital development, industry-relevant skills, and the creation of productive and decent employment opportunities.
To meet the growing demand, the higher education system has expanded significantly, with student enrolment reaching an all-time high of 4.5 crore in 2023-24, up from 3.42 crore in 2014-15. The gross enrolment ratio for ages 18 to 23 has also increased to 30% for the first time, reflecting improved access to higher education. As a result, the new challenge that emerged is converting this quantitative expansion into quality, employability and equitable opportunities by aligning education and skills with the requirements of the labour market.
Thus, in recent times, India's unemployment challenge has become increasingly complex. The number of educated young people entering the labour market has been increasing over the years. The rapidly evolving labour market landscape, particularly in the wake of artificial intelligence, has further widened the gap between the skills graduates possess and those that employers increasingly demand.
The Information Technology sector has been a major source of employment for young graduates. But in recent times, the IT sector itself has been under tremendous pressure. It is undergoing significant transformation, with traditional entry-level roles becoming increasingly constrained by automation, artificial intelligence and ever-changing industry requirements. Thus, there is a fundamental shift in hiring practices, moving away from legacy mass recruitment toward highly specialised, capability-led hiring. Primarily driven by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, cloud modernisation, and infrastructure growth.
However, approximately six million tech professionals are employed in the IT sector. Despite growing fears of automation and global headwinds, the IT industry continues to be a net job creator, adding 1,35,000 new jobs in the past year. On the other hand, Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India employ over 1.9 million professionals and are expected to increase in the coming years. At the same time, hiring is expected to shift from volume to skill mix, to pass on AI-driven productivity gains to clients.
While the above-stated reasons reflect the dynamics of the labour market, unemployment and underemployment are deeply rooted in long-standing structural issues and are not new phenomena. Primarily, low household incomes, underemployment, apparent skill gaps, and a widespread casual workforce lead to low productivity across sectors of the economy. Therefore, the measured unemployment rate does not mean that the underlying employment problems have been resolved. The real challenge is to ensure that India’s growing workforce moves from unemployment or low-productivity jobs into stable, productive, and adequately remunerated employment.
Thus, in India, the issue of people not having jobs is not the only problem; it runs much deeper than it appears, hidden in the employment statistics. The main issue is that India has been facing challenges in creating enough productive, well-paid, and suitable jobs for its large and increasingly educated workforce. As we witness, needy people typically move from being willingly unemployed to low-paid, informal, self-employed, or under-employed work without experiencing a proportional improvement in their economic well-being.
Improving employment opportunities for qualified youth requires not only skill upgradation but also stronger alignment with the industry's evolving needs. Educational institutions should focus on imparting practical, job-relevant skills and expanding opportunities for work-based learning through industry projects and internships. Thus, educational institutions need to establish closer collaboration with industry, and industry needs to be more proactive in providing sufficient opportunities for young graduates.
At the same time, creating more high-quality jobs that offer meaningful career progression, competitive wages, and opportunities for continuous learning is essential to ensure that employment opportunities match the skills and aspirations of the growing educated workforce.
The fundamental reason for underemployment and rising unemployment among young graduates is that the labour market hasn’t followed the usual path of workers from agricultural jobs to industrial employment. Instead, it skipped manufacturing entirely and moved directly into office and service-related employment.
This structural shift has left millions of ordinary people still engaged in casual and day labour because there aren’t sufficient factories to hire them, and they lack the high-tech skills required for modern office work. Therefore, India has been facing a unique situation in which robust economic growth does not automatically translate into increased job opportunities. This explains the disconnect between official job data and reality: widespread underemployment and economic uncertainty stemming from geopolitical tensions make the unemployment crisis feel far more acute than the numbers indicate.
Gross Fixed Capital Formation is a measure of investments in productive assets, which in turn generate employment opportunities. India’s capital formation has increased significantly, reaching 34.3% of GDP in 2025-26, above the pre-pandemic average of 28.6%. This reflects a substantial expansion of productive capacity in recent years. However, increased investments in productive assets do not necessarily imply corresponding employment generation. The impact of growing investment on employment primarily depends on the sectors in which the investment is made. Unless investments in labour-intensive sectors increase, we cannot expect a proportionate increase in employment.
India Skills Report 2026 recommended that reducing the graduate unemployment rate requires shifting from giving educational credentials to developing job-ready skills that match changing employer demand. Nevertheless, the report noted that overall youth employability rose to 56.35% from 54.81% in its previous edition. This improvement has been attributed to the acquisition of skills such as artificial intelligence, digital skills, gig work, freelancing, and remote work, as well as a growing culture of entrepreneurship among the youth.
Therefore, it is necessary to shift from a degree-centric education system to a dynamic skill ecosystem that ensures continuous upskilling and reskilling in response to ever-changing technological advancements. The way forward lies in a stronger, closer connection among industry, academia, experiential learning, and AI-enabled education to enhance the employability of graduates. At the same time, developing human skills such as creativity, critical thinking, and adaptability is equally essential for enhancing the job fitness of young graduates.
M. Venkateshwarlu is a Professor of Finance at the Indian Institute of Management Mumbai.

India and the US have concluded most of the discussions for a proposed bilateral trade pact, and they are now fine-tuning the agreement, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday.
"We have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement," he said while talking about the India-US trade agreement. The minister is in The Hague on a two-day official visit. He is accompanying a business delegation.

China has defended the movement of its troops along the India-China border, saying its patrols are aimed at protecting territorial sovereignty and maintaining stability. The response comes following the reports of fresh face-offs between Indian security forces and Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday that Beijing had consistently followed the agreements and important understandings reached with New Delhi. According to China's Global Times, Guo said Chinese forces were carrying out routine patrols and management activities in the border areas.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
Responding to reports of another confrontation along the frontier, Guo said China and India remained in contact through diplomatic and military channels. He urged New Delhi to work with Beijing to implement the existing understandings and take steps to preserve peace along the border.
The remarks followed a statement by India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), which said disturbances occurred when Chinese troops deviated from established patrolling patterns. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said both countries continued to rely on existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to address unresolved issues and prevent misunderstandings along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
Fresh Face-Offs Reported In Arunachal Pradesh
The exchange of statements comes amid renewed attention on the disputed frontier in Arunachal Pradesh. Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) chief Shatrujeet Kapur confirmed on Thursday that face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops were continuing at several locations.
His remarks followed reports of a stand-off in the Asaphila area that had reportedly been underway since late July. The latest developments have brought the sensitive border sector back into focus, despite efforts by both countries to stabilise relations.
According to a source in New Delhi cited in Deccan Herald, the current situation is linked to a dispute that began in 2023. The source alleged that China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) had blocked Indian Army personnel from accessing the Shera 5 patrolling point near Taksing, in the Upper Subansiri district of Arunachal Pradesh.
The location lies near the sensitive Asaphila sector along the LAC. The reported restriction on Indian patrol access has remained a concern, according to the source.
Arunachal Pradesh Naming Row Adds To Tensions
The military developments come against the backdrop of a continuing disagreement over Arunachal Pradesh. India considers the state an integral part of its territory, while China refers to it as Zangnan, or South Tibet, and claims sovereignty over the region.
The dispute intensified again after India formally named 27 geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh. Beijing objected to the move in August, describing India's naming exercise as illegal and void and maintaining that it would not affect China's territorial claims.
The competing claims over geographical names reflect the wider disagreement between the two countries over the boundary. Neither official statements nor efforts to manage military encounters have resolved the underlying dispute.
The latest developments also highlight how the tensions extend beyond troop movements, involving competing territorial claims, maps and infrastructure along the frontier.
Modi-Xi Meeting May Take Place At G20 Summit
The renewed focus on the border comes as speculation grows over another possible meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
According to Deccan Herald, the two leaders may meet again on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Florida, the United States, on December 14 or 15. US President Donald Trump is scheduled to host the summit in Miami.
The possibility of another meeting comes after Modi and Xi held talks on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12.
However, subsequent developments have complicated that assessment. Beijing has reiterated its claims over the Shaksgam Valley, an area India considers its territory and says Pakistan illegally ceded to China in 1963. China has also asserted sovereignty over the entire western sector of the India-China boundary, Deccan Herald reported.
Despite these differences, sources cited by the newspaper said New Delhi remained inclined to continue its renewed engagement with Beijing.
The diplomatic outreach follows the October 2024 agreement that brought an end to the 4.5-year-long military stand-off in eastern Ladakh. However, the latest reports from Arunachal Pradesh underline that the wider border dispute remains unresolved, even as both sides continue diplomatic efforts to prevent tensions from escalating.

articles.summary: Kazakhstan and UAE Advance Trans-Afghan Railway to Connect Central Asia With Pakistani Ports  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the United Arab Emirates have signed a strategic agreement to advance the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA) railway, an infrastructure corridor designed to link landlocked Eurasian markets with seaports in Pakistan. The proposed route through Afghanistan aims to handle up to 10 million tonnes of cargo annually, diversifying Central Asia's trade networks beyond the existing Middle Corridor and traditional Russian routes. The project reflects a broader geoeconomic shift as Central Asian republics actively seek independent maritime access.
The CASA railway agreement
The memorandum of cooperation, signed on September 30, 2026, by the transport ministries of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan alongside the UAE’s Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, formally initiates the technical and economic assessment of the trans-Afghan corridor. The project represents a fundamental shift in regional logistics, offering the landlocked republics a direct southern outlet to the Arabian Sea via the Pakistani ports of Karachi and Gwadar. The participating governments have committed to establishing a dedicated working group to evaluate the required railway infrastructure, outline logistics facility upgrades, and design viable financing mechanisms.
The strategic logic behind the CASA initiative is rooted in the urgent need for trade diversification. Historically reliant on northern routes through the Russian Federation, Central Asian exporters have increasingly sought alternative pathways to global markets amid geopolitical instability and sanctions regimes. While Kazakhstan has invested heavily in the Middle Corridor—a multimodal route traversing the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to reach European markets—that pathway remains complex and subject to maritime bottlenecks. The southern route offers a continuous overland connection to the massive consumer markets of South Asia and direct access to the Indian Ocean maritime shipping lanes.
UAE’s logistical leverage
The inclusion of the United Arab Emirates as a primary partner brings crucial capital and operational expertise to a project that has struggled to move beyond the conceptual phase for years. Emirati logistics giants, such as AD Ports Group and DP World, possess extensive experience in integrating national railway networks with maritime terminals and dry ports. The UAE’s own Etihad Rail project provides a template for developing industrial clusters alongside transport corridors. By entering the Central Asian logistics sector at this early stage, the UAE is positioning itself to manage and profit from the future flow of agricultural commodities, critical minerals, and manufactured goods between Eurasia and the Gulf.
| CASA Railway Project Partners and Objectives |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Participating Nation | Primary Role | Strategic Objective | 
|---|---|---|
| Kazakhstan | Origin market and northern transit | Export diversification and access to Indian Ocean ports | 
| Uzbekistan | Regional transit hub | Integrating domestic rail networks with the Afghan border | 
| United Arab Emirates | Financing and technical logistics | Securing supply chains to Gulf markets and infrastructure revenue | 
| Pakistan | Maritime gateway | Increasing cargo throughput at Karachi and Gwadar terminals | 
Security risks and feasibility challenges
Despite the high-level political backing, the CASA railway faces formidable physical and security challenges. The route must traverse the difficult mountainous terrain of the Hindu Kush and operate securely within Afghanistan, a jurisdiction with severe infrastructure deficits and complex internal security dynamics. The estimated capacity of 10 million tonnes of annual cargo represents a theoretical projection of regional trade demand rather than a guaranteed immediate throughput. The ultimate viability of the corridor depends on aligning the transit tariffs, customs protocols, and border management procedures of four distinct national governments operating under vastly different regulatory frameworks.
The initiative has drawn significant attention from European powers seeking to secure stable supply chains for critical raw materials. Germany has expressed a distinct strategic interest in the development of Central Asian transport links. During a meeting in Astana on October 23, Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister Serik Zhumangarin and German Ambassador Heike Peitsch discussed the expansion of the southern route and its potential to bridge European and Asian markets. The bilateral dialogue, which followed President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Germany, underscored that European economies view the diversification of Eurasian transport corridors as a necessary component of their own economic security.
The successful implementation of the CASA railway would cement Kazakhstan’s role as the primary logistics hub of the Eurasian landmass. By developing the southern corridor in tandem with its Caspian Sea infrastructure, the government in Astana aims to provide domestic exporters with the flexibility to pivot between European, Middle Eastern, and Asian markets based on prevailing economic conditions. However, the immediate task for the newly formed working group is to translate diplomatic memorandums into bankable engineering studies that can attract the billions of dollars required to lay track across one of the world's most challenging geopolitical landscapes.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday ruled out an immediate military strike against Iran, saying Washington had no plans to launch an attack that day, even as conflicting intelligence assessments and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts continued to shape the US approach to Tehran.
"Would I tell you that? But the answer is no. There will not be a strike," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Michigan, responding to a question about whether military action against Iran could take place as soon as Sunday.
"We have two very different sets of intelligence reports," Trump said, describing the incoming information as "very advanced."
The president maintained that Washington was doing "well with Iran," although an unnamed US official told Israeli news channel i24NEWS that Trump was prepared to "shift gears on Iran" and that military strikes no longer appeared to be "a question of if, but of when."
The remarks came after Trump presented Tehran with a stark choice between reaching a diplomatic agreement and facing further military action.
"Do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off? That's the only question," Trump told Fox News, framing the next phase of the conflict as a choice between negotiations and escalating military operations.
Despite ruling out a strike on Sunday, Trump has continued to signal that Washington could pursue further military action if negotiations fail to produce an agreement.
Trump claims US controls Strait of Hormuz
Trump also asserted that American forces had established maritime dominance over the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route and a major point of contention in the conflict with Iran.
"Remember, we now control the Hormuz Strait. They get nothing. Yes, we get everything." He maintained that commercial activity through the chokepoint had exceeded pre-war levels and described the US Navy's enforcement of a blockade on Iranian ports and shipping as "unbelievable."
On Saturday, Trump had suggested that Washington could either launch fresh military strikes or secure a comprehensive agreement with Tehran. He questioned whether Iran would honour any commitments under a potential deal, while arguing that either outcome would amount to an American victory.
Control over the Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of friction in the conflict, which erupted in late February following joint US-Israeli strikes. The confrontation has continued despite a ceasefire and a memorandum aimed at securing a final peace agreement.
Trump signals Russia-Ukraine peace talks
Turning to the war in Eastern Europe, Trump indicated that high-level diplomatic engagements involving the United States, Russia and Ukraine could take place soon.
"We're going to be having some pretty soon, and I think they both want to make a deal," he said, expressing optimism about the prospects of negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv.
Trump did not provide further details about the proposed engagements or specify when the talks would take place.
On Brazil's presidential election, the US president refrained from endorsing either candidate, saying his administration was "watching" the race.
Trump links European unrest to immigration
Trump also criticised immigration policies in European countries, linking protests and unrest in France, Italy, Belgium and Spain to what he described as inadequate border enforcement.
Contrasting the situation in Europe with US border controls, he claimed that the United States had prevented unauthorised crossings over the preceding 18 months.
"I closed the border. You know that we've had zero infiltration," Trump said, asserting that "zero illegal aliens" had entered the country during that period. He also claimed that previous US administrations had allowed millions of people to enter illegally.
Referring to his conversations with French President Emmanuel Macron, Trump said he had previously warned the French leader about the consequences of immigration policies.
"'You are destroying France. You're letting people come in that hate your country.'" Trump said he had told Macron.
He also cited migrant arrivals in Spain as evidence of what he described as wider instability across Europe.
Trump accuses Taiwan of taking US chip industry
On semiconductor manufacturing and trade, Trump accused Taiwan of taking over the US chip industry through low-cost production, renewing his criticism of the island's position in the global semiconductor supply chain.
"They stole our chip business, all of it, 100%, because they made chips at a ridiculous price, and they just pushed them in," Trump said.
He argued that stronger executive leadership in Washington could have prevented broader tensions with China over trade and technology.
Trump's comments come amid continuing US efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing and address Washington's strategic competition with Beijing.

articles.title: If Netanyahu goes, will Israel's India policy change? - India Today
articles.summary: If Netanyahu goes, will Israel's India policy change?  India Today
articles.full_text:
Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu's friendship with PM Narendra Modi has helped deepen India and Israel's defence, technology and diplomatic ties. But as Israel votes on Tuesday, could Netanyahu's possible exit alter New Delhi's equations? What would it mean for India's investments, defence deals and ambitious connectivity projects involving Israel?
In July 2017, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu raised a toast to PM Narendra Modi at a banquet in Jerusalem, celebrating a friendship that he said had taken 70 years to reach Israel's doorstep. Nine years later, Netanyahu is fighting to remain Israel's prime minister, and India is watching the contest closely.
His friendship with PM Modi has helped transform bilateral ties, particularly in defence, intelligence, technology and diplomacy. But Israel's relationship with India now extends well beyond the two leaders. If Netanyahu, who is trailing in pre-poll surveys, loses, will New Delhi lose its special place in Israel's strategic calculations? Will the India-Israel partnership lose steam if a change of guard takes place in Jerusalem?
What would happen to India's ambitious India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), its investments in Israel's Haifa Port, defence cooperation, joint military projects and the proposed free trade agreement if Netanyahu loses power?
Israel votes on Tuesday (October 27), with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerging as Netanyahu's principal challenger. Netanyahu, who has recently identified India as a key partner in reducing Israel's dependence on the United States, appears to be prepared for a future in which Washington might become less supportive.
Eisenkot, however, has emphasised rebuilding Israel's relations with traditional Western partners. That raises the important question about whether India would enjoy the same diplomatic prominence under a new Israeli government, if one barring Netanyahu, comes to power?
For New Delhi, the stakes are beyond PM Modi's personal equation with Netanyahu. Israel is a major defence and technology partner, while India's equally good relationships with Iran and all the Gulf countries make regional stability important.
HOW MODI AND NETANYAHU BUILT A SPECIAL RELATIONSHIP
India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in January 1992, long before Modi and Netanyahu developed their personal rapport. But Modi's July 2017 visit to Israel, the first by an Indian prime minister, brought the relationship into the public spotlight.
Welcoming Modi, Netanyahu said, "We've waited for you for 70 years."
The visit was marked by unusually warm personal diplomacy, including the two leaders' much-publicised walk along the Mediterranean coast. In January 2018, Netanyahu reciprocated with a visit to India.
The test of the relationship was evident during Operation Sindoor, when India struck terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir following the Pahalgam attack. Israel was among the countries that openly backed India's right to self-defence. Israeli Ambassador Reuven Azar said, "Israel supports India's right to self-defence. Terrorists should know there's no place to hide from their heinous crimes against the innocent."
The partnership expanded further during Modi's February 2026 visit to Israel, when the two countries elevated relations to a Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity. The agreements covered defence, artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, semiconductors, agriculture and other emerging technologies.
These institutional arrangements are why India and Israel are likely to remain close, regardless of who comes to power in Israel.
NETANYAHU LOOKS AT INDIA FOR POST-TRUMP AMERICA
On October 18, just nine days before the election, Netanyahu presented a security doctrine that revealed how prominently India figures in his post-Donald Trump diplomatic calculations. Warning that a future American president could be hostile towards Israel, Netanyahu argued for strengthening alternative partnerships.
"The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others," Netanyahu said. The remarks are significant because the US remains Israel's principal military and diplomatic backer.
Netanyahu has also pointed to Latin America as another region where Israel could cultivate new partnerships. In May 2026, he described India as a "huge power" and spoke of the "absolutely crazy love for Israel" in the country.
However, Netanyahu's main challenger, Eisenkot, has criticised the prime minister's October 18 security doctrine. He accused Netanyahu of presenting slogans rather than a credible strategy.
Unlike Netanyahu, Eisenkot has not publicly outlined a detailed India-specific policy. His broader foreign-policy stresses on "repairing" Israel's international relationships.
WILL INDIA-ISRAEL TIES OUTLAST NETANYAHU?

articles.title: China Salami-Slicing Border To Force India To Accept The Rejected 1959 Line – Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: China Salami-Slicing Border To Force India To Accept The Rejected 1959 Line – Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- ITBP chief Kapur reported recent face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh and called China India’s “biggest adversary,” while the government dismissed them as normal and the opposition questioned improving ties.
- China seeks to advance the 1959 LAC through salami-slicing; after 1962 it withdrew in the east but kept ~38,000 sq km of Aksai Chin, with later pacts managing but not resolving the line.
- Experts say China prefers military consolidation of the 1959 line over talks, and India’s 1960 rejection of swapping Aksai Chin for Arunachal Pradesh remains politically unviable.
At a time when India and China are beginning to put their decades-old border dispute on the back burner to help boost trade and investment instead, border tensions have surfaced again.
The Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), Shatrujeet Kapur, said last Thursday that in the past few-days, a situation had arisen where face-offs were happening at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh.
Kapur said that the China front was the “most difficult” border. “Powerful” China was India’s “biggest adversary,” requiring enhanced capabilities to “counter” it.
The ITBP, raised in 1962, after the Sin-Indian war, guards the 3,488-km-long Line of Actual Control (LAC) from Ladakh in the North to Arunachal Pradesh in the East.
The ITBP chief however added that a new combat team, the Shaurya Commandos, had displayed its skills during the “ongoing” faceoff with Chinese troops at multiple places in Arunachal Pradesh. These commandos would be in every IRBP battalion, he added.
While an embarrassed Indian government dismissed the faceoffs as normal on the yet undefined LAC, opposition parties and independent media said that the faceoffs cast doubts on the government’s consistent claim that Sino-India relations are on the mend. The opposition demanded to know if India was being bullied by both the US and China.
The reported incidents on the LAC are not new. China has been claiming the India State of Arunachal Pradesh for decades, saying that traditionally it has been part of the Tibet region of China. Beijing has been issuing special visas to persons from Arunachal Pradesh and giving new names to villages in that State.
The Bottom Line is China’s Claim to the 1959 Line
It is clear that even if China does not seek the absorption of the whole of Arunachal Pradesh, it wants to go back to the LAC proposed by Premier Zhou Enlai to the Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru in a letter dated November 7, 1959, a proposal that has been unacceptable to India.
Through “salami slicing” tactics, the Chinese are incrementally but continually pushing the Indians to accept the 1959 line as the LAC.
The concept of an LAC was introduced by Zhou in a 1959 letter to Jawaharlal Nehru as the “line up to which each side exercises actual control”. Zhou proposed that the armed forces of the two sides should withdraw 20 kilometres from the McMahon Line in the East and the line up to which each side exercises actual control in the West. But this was rejected by Nehru as being historically untenable.
On November 21, 1962, after decisively defeating Indian forces, Premier Zhou Enlai announced a unilateral ceasefire and that Chinese forces would withdraw 20 km behind the Line of Actual Control as it existed on November 7, 1959 – not the 1962 fighting line. The 1959 LAC was China’s own claim line as shown on maps Zhou had sent to Nehru in 1959. China was asking India to also keep its forces 20 km behind that same 1959 LAC to create a 40 km demilitarized zone, patrolled by neither side.
But India did not withdraw because its forward posts had already been overrun and its troops had retreated in disarray. India also rejected that concept outright, calling the 1959 line an illegal claim. Nehru said India would not be bound by a unilateral Chinese definition of the LAC.
The result was two different stories in East and West. In the Eastern Sector China withdrew almost completely. It vacated all the territory it had occupied south of the McMahon Line during the war – places like Tawang, Bomdila, Walong – and went back to the north side of the McMahon Line. Net territorial gain for China in the East was nil. In fact, it returned to status quo ante.
In the Western Sector, China kept its gains. Before 1962, India claimed Aksai Chin and had established 43 forward posts, including in areas China already controlled. During the war, China overran all of them. When China “withdrew 20 km behind the 1959 LAC”, in the West, the 1959 LAC was already deep inside what India claimed, roughly along the line China controls today.
So China did not withdraw to pre-1960 positions after the war. It retained about 38,000 sq km of Aksai Chin that it had controlled since the 1950s and consolidated in 1962. India lost the ability to patrol up to its claimed line. The practical LAC after 1962 moved westward in India’s view.
The term “LAC” gained legal recognition in Sino-Indian agreements signed in 1993 and 1996. The 1996 agreement states, “No activities of either side shall overstep the line of actual control. In October 2013, India and China signed a border defence cooperation agreement to ensure that patrolling along the LAC does not escalate into armed conflict.
In October 2024, India announced that it had reached an agreement over patrolling arrangements along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the border area, which would lead to disengagement and resolution of the long-running conflict that began in 2020.
On 30 July 2020, the Chinese Ambassador to India, Sun Weidong, stated that China was not in favour of clarifying the LAC anymore as it would create new disputes. Similar viewpoints were aired in India that China will keep the boundary dispute alive for as long as it can be used against India.
Speaking to ThePrint in a video interview, Dr. Yun Sun Senior Fellow and Director of the China Program at the Stimson Center said: “We can see that China is probably aiming for their Line of Actual Control back in 1959. What happened between 1959 and 1962 according to Chinese perception was an Indian ‘forward policy’ that advanced towards the Chinese territory, which eventually led to the 1962 war. That’s a very Chinese-centric, Sino-centric perception. But that’s how China has viewed this territorial dispute in the historical perspective.”
“Political negotiations are unlikely to go anywhere,” she said. “They have not rendered a concrete result, which means the LAC can only be consolidated on the ground by the pulling and hauling, by the positioning of the military troops, so that the two militaries would develop a consensus as for where the other side is firmly stationed.”
Yun, who analyses the policies of the Chinese government, also believes that the present standoff between the Indian and Chinese troops may not lead to a full-fledged hot war but will turn into a “war of attrition”.
Meanwhiike, Gen. M.M.Naravane, who served as India’s Army chief from 2019 to 2022, has suggested that India and China consider the 1959 Chinese proposal to barter the disputed territories of Aksai Chin and Arunachal Pradesh to end the border dispute. But India had rejected thi sis 1960 itself.
Gen. Naravane recalled that in 1959-60, Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai had told his Indian counterpart Jawaharlal Nehru that the two countries should barter Aksai Chin and Arunachal Pradesh. “Aksai Chin is theirs, and Arunachal Pradesh is ours. Perhaps this could be the solution. The nitty-gritty can be discussed to mutual satisfaction,” the General said. He added that the idea had come up several times during Sino-Indian discussions on the border issue but had been put on the back burner.
But India had rejected the Chinese proposal to barter Aksai Chin for Arunachal Pradesh in 1960.
According to Srinath Raghavan, the Chinese were interested only in specific areas in the Eastern and Western sectors. But India would not agree to any of these because, in its view, China’s territorial ambitions tended to be ever-growing.
Sino-Indian relations have deteriorated so much since 1960-62, and Indian nationalism has reached such heights now, that it will be futile to talk about reviving the barter proposal now.

articles.title: Lok Sabha Speaker urges BRICS parliaments to champion ethical, responsible, and transparent technology with Paramount human oversight - India's News.Net

New Delhi [India], October 26 (ANI): Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla urged BRICS parliaments to champion ethical, responsible and transparent technology with paramount human oversight, according to a press release issued by the Lok Sabha Secretariat.
Addressing the plenary sessions of the ongoing 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum, Birla said BRICS nations, representing approximately half of the world's population, shared a collective responsibility to use technology ethically while safeguarding parliamentary sovereignty and fostering cooperation, the press release stated.
Earlier in the day, Birla inaugurated the forum, according to the Lok Sabha Secretariat.
The press release said Birla outlined several digital innovations introduced by the Parliament of India to improve legislative capacity, transparency, efficiency and public access. These include secure digital platforms that provide MPs online access to questions and answers, along with prompt responses from government departments.
He also highlighted multilingual initiatives offering the daily List of Business in 10 languages, with work underway to extend it to all 22 scheduled languages, as well as simultaneous interpretation in 22 languages.
According to the press release, Birla highlighted the digitisation of pre- and post-independence parliamentary debates, equipped with metadata and video-search facilities, alongside round-the-clock online access to research papers and home delivery of books from the Parliament Library.
The Lok Sabha Secretariat said he also discussed paperless governance initiatives using the National e-Vidhan Application (NeVA) and the 'One Nation, One Legislative Platform', which connect legislatures and enable live streaming of proceedings, debates, budgets and law-making information.
Birla highlighted India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), which empowers citizens, promotes financial inclusion and facilitates transparent benefit transfers directly into bank accounts to reduce corruption. He stressed that advanced technology must remain responsible, accountable and human-centric, aligned with ethical values, human sensitivities and dignity.
On the sidelines of the forum, Birla hosted UAE Federal National Council Speaker Saqr Ghobash. According to the press release, the leaders reaffirmed historic bonds of friendship and discussed strengthening parliamentary cooperation through regular dialogue, delegation exchanges and sharing best practices in digital governance, artificial intelligence, committee functioning and the Online Assurance Monitoring System.
They also discussed expanding cooperation in trade, investment, education, youth exchanges and people-to-people connections, aligning with the shared aspirations of Viksit Bharat and We the UAE 2031, while emphasising regional peace and stability through diplomacy.
Later, Birla met Zheng Jianbang, Vice Chairman of China's National People's Congress. The two leaders discussed strengthening bilateral relations through parliamentary exchanges and cooperation in education, healthcare and technology.
Birla emphasised the shared responsibility of India and China to maintain peace and tranquillity along the border and resolve differences amicably through dialogue and mutual respect. He also highlighted parliamentary diplomacy, trade relations and people-to-people ties, expressing confidence that Parliamentary Friendship Groups and multilateral platforms such as BRICS would deepen mutual understanding.
The Lok Sabha Secretariat further stated that Birla met Ahmed Naderi, Member of the Praesidium of Iran's Islamic Consultative Assembly. Recalling historical ties and high-level engagements, including their meeting in September 2026, Birla stressed the importance of peace and stability in West Asia.
The two sides discussed advancing cooperation on Chabahar Port through joint efforts. Naderi expressed gratitude for the medicines, assistance and other support extended by India to Iran, while both sides reaffirmed the importance of continued engagement to strengthen longstanding bilateral ties, the press release said. (ANI)

articles.title: Ritu Choudhary’s China Infiltration Claim Sparks Row: India… - theopenpress.in
articles.summary: Ritu Choudhary’s China Infiltration Claim Sparks Row: India…  theopenpress.in
articles.full_text:
A viral video, a claim of Chinese infiltration and an official Army clarification have triggered a fresh debate over how national security incidents are presented on social media. Congress spokesperson Ritu Choudhary shared footage linked to an alleged Chinese intrusion near the India-China border, raising questions about the government’s handling of border security.
However, the Indian Army has disputed the interpretation of the footage. According to its official fact-check, the video shows Chinese commercial vehicles operating at the authorised border trade point at Nathu La in Sikkim—not evidence of an unauthorised Chinese military intrusion.
The clarification has shifted attention towards a crucial question: when a video appears to show activity near an international border, how can viewers distinguish a genuine security incident from a misleading claim?
What Does the Viral Video Actually Show?
The footage circulating on social media showed JAC-branded commercial trucks alongside vehicles associated with the Indian Army. Some posts claimed that Chinese vehicles had entered Indian territory without authorisation. The footage was also used to question the government’s approach to border security.
But the presence of Chinese-branded vehicles does not, by itself, establish that a military intrusion has taken place. The location, purpose of the vehicles and rules governing movement in the area are essential to understanding what the footage shows.
That distinction lies at the centre of the controversy surrounding the video.
Indian Army’s Fact-Check: The Nathu La Trade Route
The Indian Army’s official fact-check unit said the footage showed JAC commercial vehicles at Nathu La Pass in Sikkim, a designated India-China border trade point.
According to the Army, commercial activity at Nathu La takes place under established arrangements, designated trading facilities and regulated procedures. It said the movement of commercial vehicles on an authorised trade route was being misrepresented as evidence of an unauthorised Chinese military intrusion.
The Army urged social media users to verify the original footage, location and official context before sharing claims involving national security. It also pointed to a pattern of similar misleading posts being circulated by multiple accounts.
The central issue, therefore, is not simply what appears in the video, but whether the description accompanying it accurately reflects the activity shown.
Why Has Ritu Choudhary’s Post Become Controversial?
Choudhary linked the video to alleged Chinese infiltration and questioned the central government and the BJP over the matter. Her post drew criticism from those who argued that footage of authorised commercial activity should not be presented as proof of a military incursion.
The controversy highlights an important distinction. Criticism of the government’s border policy is part of political debate. However, a specific allegation of unauthorised entry requires evidence and an accurate understanding of the incident.
Based on the Army’s clarification, the Nathu La footage does not establish the claim that Chinese military vehicles had illegally entered Indian territory.
Retired Military Officers Raise Concerns
The video also drew critical reactions from retired military officers, bringing greater attention to the risks of sharing military-related footage without sufficient context.
Border-related videos can be difficult to interpret without information about the recording date, location, vehicle identity and operational circumstances. A short clip may show only a small part of an activity, leaving out details necessary to understand what actually happened.
This is why verification is particularly important when footage is used to make claims about territorial security or military operations.
Nathu La: Why the Trade Context Matters
Located in Sikkim, Nathu La is a designated route for border trade between India and China. Commercial movement at an authorised trade point must be distinguished from military activity or an alleged security breach.
A Chinese commercial vehicle operating under an authorised arrangement is not the same as a Chinese military vehicle entering Indian territory without permission. The two claims require different evidence and should not be treated as interchangeable.
The Army’s clarification provides the context needed to assess the specific video, while broader questions about border security must be examined through reliable information and official statements.

Read More: India-China Border Talks: Ajit Doval and Wang Yi Agree on Early Harvest and New Military Hotlines
The Bigger Lesson: Verify Before Sharing
The Nathu La controversy underlines how quickly a video can acquire a misleading interpretation once it is shared with an inaccurate or incomplete caption. In matters involving the armed forces and national security, such claims can create unnecessary confusion and public anxiety.
Before forwarding similar footage, users should check its original source, recording date, location and any official clarification. They should also distinguish political allegations from facts established by reliable evidence.
In this case, the Indian Army has said the footage showed commercial vehicles at an authorised border trade point. That clarification is central to understanding the controversy—and a reminder that a compelling video is not necessarily proof of the claim attached to it.

Protests against a proposed Himalayan dam in India’s Arunachal Pradesh state turned violent, leaving around 40 police personnel injured. Demonstrators also torched buildings and vandalised government offices while opposing the major hydropower project.
The unrest erupted over the proposed 11,200-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, planned by state-run hydropower company NHPC. Chief Minister Pema Khandu said protesters damaged public property, attacked a police station and ransacked homes belonging to elected representatives. Police fired tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Khandu urged opponents to raise their concerns through dialogue rather than violence. He called on local communities to question the government and discuss the project peacefully. However, resistance remains strong among residents who fear the dam could displace families and destroy their land.
India says the project is needed to counter China’s planned $167 billion Yaxia hydropower scheme in Tibet. New Delhi fears the Chinese project could affect water flows downstream into the Brahmaputra River. Indian officials say their proposed dam would create a large reservoir to store water and help maintain river flows.
Beijing has said its hydropower project will have no negative impact on downstream areas. China also claims Arunachal Pradesh, which it calls Zangnan, as part of South Tibet. India has repeatedly rejected that territorial claim, adding to tensions between the neighbouring countries.
The dispute highlights wider tensions between India and China, which share a contested Himalayan border guarded by thousands of troops. India’s foreign ministry said both countries remained in regular contact to manage border tensions. The statement followed reports from a senior Indian border police official about recent face-offs between their forces.

articles.title: Israel elections: Can Benjamin Netanyahu turn security gains into a political victory? - The Times of India
articles.summary: Israel elections: Can Benjamin Netanyahu turn security gains into a political victory?  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Three years after the October 7 attack, 
Benjamin Netanyahu
 faces a crucial electoral test over security, political accountability and the direction of Israel.
Donald Trump’s endorsement and the unresolved confrontation with Iran have raised the stakes, but a divided opposition may struggle to turn its challenge into power.
Israelis vote on Tuesday, October 27, in the country's first general election since Hamas's October 7, 2023, terrorist attack. The outcome could determine whether Bibi, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, extends his political career or loses power after three years of war and domestic turmoil.
The final opinion polls suggest a close contest. Surveys published by Israel's three major television networks on Friday put Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party ahead of Netanyahu's Likud. Yet neither the prime minister's coalition nor the main opposition bloc is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Yashar was projected to win around 22-23 seats, against 19-21 for Likud. Netanyahu's coalition was projected at about 50 seats, while the main opposition bloc was estimated at 52-56. Arab-led parties could win another 14-16 seats.
These are projections, not results. But they point to the central question of the election: can Netanyahu survive the verdict on his leadership and can his opponents agree on an alternative?
The challenger: Gadi Eisenkot
Eisenkot, a former chief of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF), has emerged as Netanyahu's principal challenger. 
He served as military chief from 2015 to 2019 and joined the wartime government formed after the October 7 attack.
He left the government in June 2024, arguing that political considerations were influencing decisions on the war. He subsequently broke with Benny Gantz and established Yashar in September 2025.
Eisenkot's appeal rests on military experience, greater accountability and the argument that Israel needs a change of leadership without abandoning its security priorities.
He is not a conventional left-wing challenger. His criticism centres on Netanyahu's handling of the war, the failures that preceded October 7 and the government's domestic agenda. Like several other opposition figures, he takes a hard line on Hamas and argues that Israel needs more effective security leadership.
This distinction matters. The election is not a straightforward contest between hawkish and dovish approaches. Many of Netanyahu's opponents argue that his decisions have weakened Israel's security rather than strengthened it.
October 7 and accountability
The October 7 attack remains the defining test of Netanyahu's leadership.
Hamas-led militants killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel and took 251 hostages, according to Israeli figures. The attack exposed major failures in intelligence, military preparedness and the government's assessment of Hamas's intentions.
Netanyahu has emphasised the military campaigns that followed, presenting his government as determined to dismantle Hamas and confront threats from Iran and its regional allies. His critics argue that the attack happened under his watch and that the government has yet to provide an adequate account of how Israel's security establishment failed to prevent it.
Opposition parties and critics have demanded an independent state commission of inquiry. Netanyahu has resisted such an investigation, which could scrutinise decisions taken by his government as well as the military and intelligence services.
In recent weeks, reports said he had advance warning from the UAE and Egypt that Hamas was planning an attack. He calls the claims libellous and is taking legal action against the outlets that published them.
His personal legal troubles add another layer. Netanyahu is on trial on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which he denies. In November 2025, he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon without admitting guilt, following public pressure from Trump. The trial remains a separate legal process.
He is also subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Gaza, which he rejects.
For his supporters, Netanyahu remains an experienced leader facing extraordinary security challenges. For his opponents, his political survival has become inseparable from questions of accountability.
Dr Ashok Sharma, a visiting fellow at the University of New South Wales in Canberra, said the October 7 attacks had damaged Netanyahu's reputation as Israel's most experienced security-oriented leader. However, he cautioned against underestimating the prime minister's political resilience.
“His supporters increasingly assess his leadership through Israel’s subsequent military campaigns against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran,” Sharma said, adding that these operations had demonstrated Israel's military capabilities and determination to confront regional threats.
For conservative and nationalist voters, he said, security remains a priority. The election will test whether accountability for October 7 outweighs confidence in Netanyahu's ability to confront continuing threats.
Iran war: Security asset or political liability?
Security is Netanyahu's central campaign argument and Iran is where it has become most consequential.
Israel and the United States launched military operations against Iran on February 28, targeting its nuclear and military infrastructure.
The conflict widened into a regional confrontation before a Pakistan-mediated process produced a ceasefire arrangement and a memorandum of understanding in June.
The pause has not resolved the underlying disputes. Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz remain sources of tension, while pressure on Iranian ports and continuing regional uncertainty have kept the risk of renewed fighting alive.
Netanyahu has presented the campaign against Iran as a strategic achievement, arguing that military action has weakened a major threat to Israel. He maintains that further action may be necessary to prevent Tehran from rebuilding its capabilities or pursuing a nuclear weapon.
But the war also raises questions about its costs, its long-term results and whether military operations have delivered a sustainable outcome.
Sharma said the campaign had demonstrated Israel's intelligence capabilities, technological superiority and ability to project military power. However, he cautioned that Iran retained the capacity for asymmetric retaliation and could rebuild its military capabilities.
“Military achievements alone cannot guarantee lasting security,” he said, arguing that the campaign's ultimate success would depend on whether military gains could be translated into sustainable deterrence, diplomatic arrangements and regional stability.
The conflict has also highlighted Israel's dependence on American military assistance, intelligence cooperation and diplomatic support. Sharma described this as a strategic partnership rather than simply a vulnerability, while noting that the long-term outcome would depend on how effectively Israel converts its military gains into lasting security.
A Financial Times report published earlier this week added a new dimension to the election.
Citing people familiar with the plans, it reported that Netanyahu had instructed the Israeli military to prepare a major offensive against Iran for the weekend of October 10. The newspaper said Trump opposed restarting the fighting before the November 3 US midterm elections. Netanyahu subsequently rejected the account as incorrect and biased.
The episode highlights a central question for Israeli voters: how much freedom does Netanyahu have to pursue his preferred military strategy without American backing?
The US is Israel's most consequential international partner, providing military assistance and diplomatic support. Even when the two governments agree on the threat posed by Iran, they may differ over the timing and consequences of further attacks.
For Netanyahu, the Iran campaign supports his longstanding argument that Israel needs a leader prepared to take decisive action. His opponents can counter that successive rounds of military escalation and ceasefires do not amount to a durable security strategy.
A change of government would not necessarily bring a major shift in policy. Eisenkot and other opposition figures have also taken a hard line on Iran and have mostly attacked Netanyahu from the right, calling him soft on security.
Hence, the difference may lie less in whether Israel regards Tehran as a threat than in how a new government chooses to manage it.
Trump backs Netanyahu — but the relationship has limits
Trump has made his preference clear. On October 18, he publicly endorsed Netanyahu's re-election, praising him as a strong leader and arguing that another prime minister might leave Washington to confront Iran alone.
Netanyahu has used the endorsement to reinforce his claim that his personal relationship with Trump helps protect Israeli interests.
Sharma said the endorsement strengthened Netanyahu's image as an internationally experienced leader capable of maintaining Washington's support. He pointed to the wider record of US-Israel cooperation, including American recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital and Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, as well as the Abraham Accords.
But the relationship is not unconditional. The reported disagreement over a possible renewed offensive against Iran suggests that Washington's calculations, including the US domestic political calendar, may not always align with Netanyahu's military priorities.
Netanyahu has disputed the reporting, but the broader tension remains relevant.
Trump's endorsement also allows Netanyahu to present the election as a choice between continuity in Israel's relationship with Washington and a potentially less predictable alternative.

articles.summary: 'Looked so corrupt’: Trump questions Brazil election after Lula defeats his ally  The Times of IndiaLula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America  BBCBrazil election ‘rigged’, says Trump without citing evidence  The HinduBolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’  Al JazeeraMarkets are dismayed by Lula’s surprise win—and for good reason  The Economist
articles.full_text:
US president Donald Trump claimed Brazil’s presidential election looked “rigged” and “so corrupt” after incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated his right-wing ally Flávio Bolsonaro, raising questions over how Washington will respond to the result.
Trump, speaking to reporters as he left Washington for a campaign rally ahead of next week’s US midterm elections, criticised the counting process and a last-minute decision to extend voting hours across Brazil.
“It looked like another rigged election, frankly,” Trump said. “It was a terrible look for the world.”
Asked whether he would take any action over the result, Trump declined to commit to a response, saying he was focused on domestic politics.
“I’m not running for Brazil, I’m running for the USA,” he said. “I like Lula, I get along with him very well. I just thought it was a very bad look, the way it was tabulated — with the extension.”
Trump did not provide evidence to support his claims of irregularities. His remarks came after Flávio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, called for the runoff result to be annulled. The challenge is considered unlikely to overturn Lula’s victory.
Voting extension becomes focus of criticism
Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered voting to be extended nationwide by two hours on Sunday after both candidates sought additional time in some areas. Lula’s request followed problems involving buses transporting voters in nine states, while Bolsonaro cited heavy rain in southern Brazil.
The extension caused confusion at some polling stations, with reports that voting machines had already been switched off before officials received the order to keep voting open.
Trump described the extension as “very strange” and cited it as a reason the election had a “very bad look”. However, he did not present evidence that the decision or the vote count had altered the outcome.
Flávio Bolsonaro’s demand to annul the result echoes efforts by his father to challenge his defeat in Brazil’s previous presidential election. Jair Bolsonaro was later convicted of plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in an attempt to overturn the result.
Trump’s Latin America ambitions face a setback
Trump’s comments come as he has repeatedly claimed credit for a rightward shift in Latin American politics, pointing to victories by conservative allies across the region. Brazil’s result leaves the country under Lula, a veteran left-wing leader whose government has clashed with Washington over trade and security policy.
“In South America, it was all leaning big left — it’s all right now,” Trump told reporters last week, claiming that every candidate he had endorsed in the region had won.
He described the shift towards conservative leadership as “extremely conservative in a very positive way”.
An ally of the Bolsonaro family, Trump had backed a political direction for Brazil that would bring it closer to his administration. Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to improve ties with Washington and pursue better deals with the US, including in the strategic minerals sector.
Despite the political divide, Trump has also spoken warmly of Lula. The two leaders have previously described their personal exchanges positively despite tensions over tariffs and other policy disputes.
Lula’s victory therefore leaves Washington facing a Brazilian government that has resisted some of Trump’s economic and diplomatic pressure, even as the US president says he maintains good personal relations with the Brazilian leader.

articles.title: Sri Lanka's Economic Recovery Underscores the Geopolitics of Debt - IR Insider
articles.summary: Sri Lanka's Economic Recovery Underscores the Geopolitics of Debt  IR Insider
articles.full_text:
As Sri Lanka advances toward another $345 million in International Monetary Fund (IMF) funding following its 2022 economic crisis, its recovery underscores the growing intersection of international debt restructuring, regional power competition, and strategic influence in the Indian Ocean. However, the funding announcement comes amid continuing economic vulnerabilities, and nationwide electricity blackout on October 17, renewing attention to the infrastructure and financial pressures that the island nation continues to face.
Sri Lanka’s recovery also carries significant geopolitical implications. Its debt restructuring has involved negotiations with China, India, Japan, as well as private creditors, such as BlackRock, illustrating how sovereign debt crises can intersect with strategic competition in the Indian Ocean.
Sri Lanka’s economic crisis reached its peak in 2022, when dwindling foreign exchange reserves left the government unable to finance essential imports, including fuel, food, and medicine. Years of fiscal deficits, combined with heavy borrowing, tax cuts that reduced government revenue, and declining foreign currency earnings, contributed to mounting financial pressures. The COVID-19 pandemic further weakened tourism, an important source of foreign exchange. In April 2022, the government suspended external debt payments, effectively defaulting on its foreign obligations. The resulting shortages and public protests culminated in the resignation of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa in July.
In March 2023, the IMF approved a four-year, approximately $3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) to support economic solidity and debt sustainability. The program included fiscal reforms, changes to energy pricing, revenue mobilization, and measures to rebuild foreign reserves. Progressive tax reform was centered as a pillar of the EFF, to increase government revenue, and encourage economic growth. Anti-backsliding buffers were also implemented, especially in the form of the Governance Diagnostic Assessment (GDA), which highlights macro-critical policy vulnerabilities that impede reform objectives, that can then be corrected for. These conditions were underscored with a commitment to negotiations with external creditors to establish a sustainable path for repayment.
China’s role as a major creditor has positioned it as central to these negotiations. Chinese institutions have financed infrastructure projects in Sri Lanka, including developments associated with Hambantota Port and Colombo Port City. China’s Export-Import Bank was among the country’s principal bilateral lenders, requiring separate negotiations alongside the restructuring process coordinated by the Official Creditor Committee. In June 2024, Sri Lanka finalized a debt restructuring agreement with the committee, co-chaired by India, Japan, and France, while also reaching a separate agreement with China’s Export-Import Bank.
These negotiations demonstrated how international financial recovery depends on coordination among countries with different creditor arrangements. Although China was not a formal member of the Official Creditor Committee, it participated and contributed separately in debt restructuring negotiations as Sri Lanka worked to meet the IMF program’s requirements. The process also reflected wider debates about how bilateral and commercial creditors should share the costs of sovereign debt crises.
India’s involvement as another major creditor further shaped the response to Sri Lanka’s economic crisis. In 2022, New Delhi extended approximately $4 billion in financial assistance through credit lines and other support as Sri Lanka struggled to pay for essential imports. India subsequently co-chaired the Official Creditor Committee and supported the debt restructuring process. According to India’s Ministry of External Affairs, the country was the first creditor nation to provide financing assurances to the IMF, helping facilitate approval of the initial program.
India’s assistance occurred against the backdrop of its longstanding strategic interests in the Indian Ocean. Sri Lanka lies near important maritime shipping routes connecting Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, making its ports and infrastructure relevant to regional trade and security. India has maintained close geographic, economic, and security ties with the island, while China’s investments have expanded its commercial presence there. These relationships have placed Sri Lanka within a wider regional environment shaped by competition over infrastructure, investment, and maritime influence.
However, the countries’ involvement in Sri Lanka’s recovery reflects a range of economic and diplomatic interests beyond direct strategic competition. India, China, Japan, and other creditors have participated in different aspects of the country’s recovery, while the IMF provides a multilateral framework for financial assistance and economic reform. The United States also holds influence through its role in the IMF and its broader engagement in the Indo-Pacific, although the current financing agreement is not a bilateral U.S. aid package. Sri Lanka’s challenge has been to negotiate with these partners while maintaining working relationships across competing strategic interests.
The latest IMF agreement illustrates how these international relationships remain relevant. Approval of the additional $345 million is contingent on the presentation of Sri Lanka’s 2027 budget in line with program requirements and completion of a financing assurances review, including confirmation of multilateral partners’ contributions and adequate progress on debt restructuring. The IMF reported that Sri Lanka’s economy grew by 4.2 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026 and that official reserves reached $6.9 billion at the end of August. However, the Fund continues to identify external shocks and global economic uncertainty as risks to the recovery.
As Sri Lanka advances through the remaining stages of its IMF program, its recovery will depend on both domestic reforms and continued engagement with international creditors and partners. The country’s experience illustrates how sovereign debt restructuring can extend beyond financial negotiations, intersecting with regional strategic interests and multilateral cooperation. With the current IMF program scheduled to conclude in 2027, Sri Lanka’s next steps will provide further insight into how smaller states navigate economic vulnerability while maintaining relationships with multiple major powers.

articles.title: Sri Lanka Grapples With Vulnerability to External Shocks - https://dailyasianage.com/
articles.summary: Sri Lanka Grapples With Vulnerability to External Shocks  https://dailyasianage.com/
articles.full_text:
Sri Lanka continues to face serious economic challenges despite making considerable progress toward recovery from its devastating financial crisis in 2022. The South Asian island nation has achieved improvements in economic growth, foreign exchange reserves, and public finances. However, high public debt, rising living costs, persistent poverty, limited employment opportunities, and vulnerability to external shocks continue to place enormous pressure on the country. The central challenge is to ensure that economic recovery translates into meaningful improvements in the lives of ordinary citizens.
Sri Lanka's economic crisis reached its peak in 2022, when the country experienced severe shortages of foreign currency, fuel, cooking gas, medicines, and other essential goods. The government struggled to meet its external debt obligations, while long queues for basic necessities became a symbol of the country's economic distress. Years of fiscal mismanagement, inadequate foreign exchange reserves, declining government revenue, and external shocks contributed to the crisis. The resulting hardship triggered widespread public protests and major political changes.
Since then, the government has pursued economic reforms with support from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Measures have included tax increases, tighter fiscal management, changes to energy pricing, and the restructuring of public debt. These steps have helped restore a degree of macroeconomic stability and improve investor confidence. Nevertheless, the recovery remains incomplete, and the benefits have not reached all sections of society equally.
One of the most pressing challenges is the country's substantial public debt burden. Although debt restructuring has progressed significantly, Sri Lanka must continue to manage its repayment obligations while maintaining essential public services and investing in development. High debt-related costs restrict the government's ability to spend on education, health care, infrastructure, and social protection. Maintaining fiscal discipline without imposing excessive hardship on vulnerable households remains a difficult balancing act.
Rising living costs present another serious concern. Higher prices for food, transportation, electricity, housing, and other necessities have reduced the purchasing power of many families. 
Even when inflation slows, households may continue to struggle because prices remain considerably higher than they were before the crisis. Low-income workers, pensioners, small business owners, and families dependent on fixed incomes are particularly vulnerable. Consequently, economic recovery must be assessed not only through national growth figures but also through changes in household living standards.
Unemployment and limited economic opportunities also threaten long-term recovery. Young people need stable jobs, better wages, and opportunities to develop professional skills. However, businesses facing high operating costs, financial constraints, and uncertain demand may hesitate to expand. Many skilled workers have also considered employment abroad in search of better incomes. Although overseas employment and remittances support the economy, the departure of skilled professionals can create shortages in important sectors.
Sri Lanka's dependence on imported fuel and other essential goods makes the economy particularly vulnerable to international developments. Increases in global oil prices can raise transportation and production costs, intensify inflationary pressure, and increase demand for foreign currency. Geopolitical conflicts, disruptions to international trade, and fluctuations in global financial markets can further complicate the country's recovery. Such external pressures demonstrate the importance of building stronger foreign exchange reserves and diversifying the economy.
Tourism remains an important source of foreign exchange and employment. Sri Lanka's beaches, cultural heritage, wildlife, and natural beauty give it considerable potential to attract international visitors. However, the tourism industry remains vulnerable to political instability, security concerns, natural disasters, and changes in global travel demand. The government should invest in infrastructure, improve service standards, protect natural resources, and promote the country in new markets to strengthen tourism revenues.
Agriculture and manufacturing also deserve greater attention. Improving agricultural productivity, supporting small businesses, expanding exports, and encouraging investment in technology could help reduce dependence on imports and create employment. Farmers need reliable access to quality seeds, fertilizers, financing, and modern equipment. At the same time, manufacturers require predictable policies, efficient transportation, and access to international markets.
Another essential priority is protecting vulnerable citizens. Economic reforms may be necessary to restore financial stability, but their social costs must not be ignored. Targeted welfare programs, accessible health care, quality education, and effective food assistance can help prevent struggling families from falling deeper into poverty. Transparent administration and stronger action against corruption are equally important for rebuilding public trust.
Recent economic assessments indicate that Sri Lanka's recovery remains vulnerable to renewed international shocks. Higher energy prices and uncertainty surrounding conflicts in the Middle East could weaken growth, increase inflation, and place additional pressure on foreign exchange reserves. Although economic activity has improved, poverty remains above pre-crisis levels, demonstrating that financial stabilization alone cannot resolve the country's deeper social and economic problems.
To overcome these challenges, Sri Lanka must maintain responsible economic policies while encouraging private investment, strengthening exports, and improving public sector efficiency. The government should also simplify business regulations, expand vocational training, support entrepreneurship, and create opportunities for young people. Stronger regional cooperation with neighboring countries, including India and Bangladesh, could further promote trade, tourism, and investment.
Ultimately, Sri Lanka's economic future will depend on the government's ability to combine financial discipline with inclusive development. Economic growth must generate jobs, improve household incomes, and provide reliable public services. With consistent reforms, transparent governance, and effective social protection, the country can gradually overcome its difficulties and build a more resilient economy. The greatest test of recovery will be whether ordinary citizens can enjoy greater security, dignity, and prosperity in their daily lives.
