More than 8,000 higher education institutions and over two lakh STEM graduates annually provide a pipeline of talent for companies seeking to establish or expand operations.
Yogi also highlighted the scope for expanding the GCC ecosystem beyond its established hubs. Noida and Greater Noida remain the state’s principal technology centres, while Lucknow, Kanpur, Prayagraj and Varanasi offer opportunities for wider geographical expansion.
He also said that to attract more investment in emerging technologies, govt is advancing its State AI Mission, deep-tech hubs, an AI City and a robotics cluster.
The summit also saw 15 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) signed and five Letters of Comfort (LoCs) issued. The partnerships aim to strengthen industry-academia collaboration and align education and skills with the evolving requirements of GCCs.
The state’s Uttar Pradesh GCC Policy 2024 offers eligible investors capital subsidies of up to 25% and land subsidies of up to 50%, subject to applicable conditions, officials said.
Organised by IIT Kanpur Alumni Association in collaboration with Invest UP and HCLTech, the summit featured seven sessions on AI-first GCCs, product-led innovation, global investment, startup partnerships and workforce development. articles.title: India-China tensions in Arunachal Pradesh: From Longju to Taksing – EXPLAINED - News9live
articles.summary: India-China tensions in Arunachal Pradesh: From Longju to Taksing – EXPLAINED  News9live
articles.full_text:
The tensions in Arunachal Pradesh stem from a century-old boundary dispute, with historical claims and territorial disagreements continuing to shape relations in the region.
New Delhi: The India-China border dispute in Arunachal Pradesh has come into focus again following reports of fresh face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops along the Line of Actual Control. ITBP Director General Shatrujeet Kapur recently confirmed that face-offs had taken place at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh frontier. Earlier reports had highlighted tensions near Asaphila, close to Taksing in Upper Subansiri district, and an encounter during routine patrolling near Maja. The ITBP and the Indian Army continue to maintain a presence in forward areas to monitor the situation and prevent further escalation.
Local concerns over traditional lands
In June 2026, the Nah Welfare Society, which represents members of the Nah tribal community, alleged that China’s People’s Liberation Army had gradually expanded its presence in areas traditionally used by local residents for grazing and agriculture.
Nah Welfare Society had submitted a memorandum to the district administration. It identified locations including Oying in the Asaphila area, Paniar, Marpan, Potrang Lake and Tindingtang, claiming that local residents had lost access to some of their traditional lands. The NWS appealed to the authorities to conduct a ground survey, restore access to the affected areas and strengthen border security and infrastructure.
The allegations, however, were disputed by the Indian Army. On 29 June, the Army described media reports of Chinese encroachment and the establishment of camps inside Indian territory as incorrect and without basis.
The historical roots: From Longju to the 1962 war
The present tensions in Arunachal Pradesh have their roots in a boundary dispute that goes back more than a century. In 1914, British Indian and Tibetan representatives reached an understanding on the boundary known as the McMahon Line. India recognises this line as its international boundary in the eastern sector, while China rejects its legitimacy.
China’s control over Tibet in the early 1950s changed the strategic situation along the frontier.
A major clash took place at Longju in August 1959. On 25 August, Chinese troops opened fire on an Indian forward post. The next day, they surrounded and attacked the post, forcing Indian troops to withdraw. The incident marked an early turning point in India–China relations.
Tensions later led to the 1962 war. On 20 October, Chinese forces launched a major attack in the eastern sector, including the Namka Chu area. Fighting spread to both the eastern and western sectors. China announced a unilateral ceasefire in November, however, the boundary dispute remained unresolved and continues to affect relations between the two countries.
Understanding the boundary dispute
India and China do not have a mutually agreed and fully demarcated boundary along the entire disputed frontier. To understand the issue, it is important to distinguish between the boundary claims, official maps and the line separating areas under their control.
The McMahon Line forms the basis of India’s boundary claim in the eastern sector. The Line of Actual Control (LAC) separates areas under Indian and Chinese control, but both countries disagree on its alignment in some places. These differences can lead to face-offs when patrols enter areas both sides claim.
The Survey of India maps show India’s official territorial position, including Arunachal Pradesh as integral part of India.
China rejects the McMahon Line and claims Arunachal Pradesh, referring to it as “Zangnan” or “South Tibet”. This difference between India’s recognised boundary and the disputed alignment of the LAC is central to tensions on the Eastern frontier
The dispute over place names
The boundary dispute also extends to maps and names of places in Arunachal Pradesh. China has repeatedly assigned Chinese names to locations in Arunachal Pradesh to reinforce its territorial claim. India has rejected these moves, stating that changing place names cannot alter the region’s status as integral part of India.
On 7 August 2026, India identified 27 locations and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh by their official names on Survey of India maps. The list included villages, mountain passes, a lake and war memorial. It also included Longju, linked to the 1959 border clash, and Thag La, associated with the 1962 war. Maja, near Taksing, was also included.
The move reflects India’s effort to formally record these places within its own mapping system. While China uses renaming to reinforce its territorial claim, India maintains that such actions do not change the status of Arunachal Pradesh. The history of Longju in 1959 and the 1962 war demonstrates how an unresolved boundary dispute can escalate into armed conflict.
For India, the challenge is to maintain vigilance along the frontier while addressing local concerns and strengthening border infrastructure. At the same time, diplomatic and military communication remains important to prevent local encounters from escalating.

 as backlash intensifies over an advertisement targeting his Democratic rival, Amy Acton, and featuring her estranged mother. The cancellations come days before the November 3 midterm elections, as Ramaswamy faces criticism from Democrats and fellow Republicans over the campaign advertisement.
The Old Dog Ale House & Brewery in Delaware, Ohio, cancelled a Republican campaign event featuring Ramaswamy on Friday, according to USA Today reporter Jessie Balmert. The Ohio Republican Party said it had selected a new location for the event.
Other businesses and event hosts have also reconsidered hosting Ramaswamy's campaign tour at their venues as people are leaving one-star reviews for these sites on Google
“We’re getting calls that people don’t want him there,” a top Ohio Republican told Zeteo, a news website founded by Mehdi Hasan. The report claimed that some business owners explicitly said that they don't want public anger.
Elliot's Wood Fired Kitchen in Newark said in the comments section of a recent Facebook post that it would not host the Ohio GOP's planned event on Tuesday, Newsweek reported. 
The Ohio Republican Party's bus tour website now lists the location of the event as "to be announced."
Venues that already hosted GOP events over the weekend have received a wave of one-star Google reviews, including Kick-N-Ax in Zanesville, Izzy's in Monroe, and The Local Bar Strongsville. Some reviewers included photos of Ramaswamy at the venues.
Vivek Ramaswamy says his mother was also defamed
The controversy centres on a 60-second advertisement produced by Ramaswamy's campaign that features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and personal history.
“I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent—and it's not easy for a mother to say this—but Amy has a serious problem,” Arthur said in the advertisement. “She is a liar. She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She's lied her entire life,” she said
Acton, a former director of the Ohio Department of Health, has spoken publicly about experiencing childhood abuse and homelessness. Her brother, Philip Stearns, has defended her account of their childhood and criticized Ramaswamy for using the family's history in a political advertisement.
Arthur lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband, Cledith Arthur, was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was a child. He pleaded not guilty, was indicted by a grand jury and subsequently failed to appear in court. He later died.
Acton has said she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old.
The advertisement has prompted criticism from prominent Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who urged Ramaswamy's campaign to stop airing it. “It's wrong to run this ad,” DeWine said, describing it as “deeply, deeply troubling”.
Ramaswamy said he did not start the fight, but he is finishing it after he found himself in this fight. He said his mother was also defamed to media silence.

articles.title: India’s balancing act: Managing border tensions with China and uncertainty with the US | India News - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: India’s balancing act: Managing border tensions with China and uncertainty with the US | India News  Hindustan Times
articles.full_text:
In a conversation on Point Blank, HT's Shishir Gupta discusses India's balancing act with China and the US with Aayesha Varma, stressing strategic autonomy.
India’s relations with China and the United States demand different kinds of balance. Along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the challenge is to hold ground while keeping military and diplomatic channels open. With Washington, it is to pursue trade and energy cooperation while preparing for shifts in US policy. In a conversation on Point Blank, Hindustan Times Executive Editor Shishir Gupta discussed these pressures with senior anchor Aayesha Varma, arguing that India’s approach rests on strategic autonomy and a willingness to engage without surrendering its position.
Arunachal Pradesh: Tensions, but no immediate sign of escalation
The discussion began with remarks by the outgoing chief of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, who had referred to face-offs at multiple points in Arunachal Pradesh in July. Gupta cautioned against treating a farewell-speech comment as a complete account of the situation. National security, he said, draws on information from military, paramilitary, intelligence and other government institutions; a public statement from one official may not capture the full picture.
Gupta described the border situation as a contest between competing claims, with India maintaining that Arunachal Pradesh is an integral part of the country and China claiming the territory. Along the LAC, he said, patrols can enter areas each side considers its own, creating the risk of face-offs. He argued that such incidents do not, by themselves, mean one side has gained control or that a wider confrontation is imminent.
According to Gupta, Indian forces had taken countermeasures and established a position intended to provide leverage, while military and diplomatic talks continued at several levels. He said the matter remained unresolved, but that the two sides were holding their positions and there had been no clashes. On that basis, he assessed the likelihood of escalation as very low at the time of the interview.
That distinction matters: a standoff can be serious without immediately becoming a conflict. Gupta pointed to the long timelines involved in resolving border disputes, citing the 1986 Sumdorong Chu episode and the continuing efforts to address friction in eastern Ladakh after 2020. His message was that dialogue and a firm military posture can coexist - and that progress on the ground may take time.
Who ordered the patrols? Several explanations remain possible
Varma asked whether the Chinese patrol activity had Beijing’s approval or reflected the initiative of a local commander. Gupta said it was difficult to determine from the information available. He outlined several possibilities rather than presenting one as established fact.
One possibility, he suggested, was that local commanders might act more aggressively under pressure to demonstrate performance, particularly amid reported changes and personnel purges in China’s military leadership. Another was that instructions for more assertive patrolling had come from higher up the chain of command. He also pointed to China’s development of border villages and infrastructure, which he said could shape how both sides perceive activity along the frontier.
These were Gupta’s interpretations, not confirmed explanations for the reported face-offs. His broader point was that the command picture and motives were uncertain, while military and diplomatic communication remained active. He also said Indian forces were prepared to maintain their positions through winter conditions.
Washington: Cooperation alongside unpredictability
The conversation then turned to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India and the status of a potential trade deal, tariffs and Russian oil. Gupta described the visit as constructive, noting discussions on terrorism and the possibility of diesel supplies from Reliance’s Jamnagar refinery. He also said External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar raised India’s concerns about Pakistan.
But a positive diplomatic visit, Gupta argued, did not guarantee predictable outcomes. He characterised the trade negotiations as unfinished, saying India was looking for two things: a competitive rate compared with other countries and greater certainty that terms would not change abruptly. The broad parameters might be in place, he said, but the agreement could not be treated as settled until it was signed.
Energy added another layer. Gupta said the US was exploring interim diesel supplies from Jamnagar, while a 60-day tariff waiver offered only temporary relief. In his assessment, US decisions were strongly shaped by domestic priorities, including prices and electoral politics. That could make Washington’s policy shifts difficult for partners to anticipate.
The contrast with the China discussion is striking. On the border, India’s stated approach is tied to peace and tranquillity: Gupta said relations cannot move forward normally if that condition breaks down. With the US, the relationship is framed more around mutual interests, but trade and energy decisions remain vulnerable to changing political calculations.
Also Read: China updates visa application process for Indians, new rules now in effect
Strategic autonomy - and more options
Gupta described India’s approach as strategic autonomy: cooperating with major powers where interests align, while resisting the idea that it must choose one side. He also linked this stance to India’s ambition to represent the concerns of the Global South and prevent wider-power competition from imposing costs on developing countries.
That approach, as presented in the interview, includes broadening India’s options. Gupta pointed to potential energy links with Canada, including Alberta oil, and to a prospective trade agreement with the European Union. Diversifying partners and supply chains, he suggested, could reduce dependence on any single relationship and give India more room to manoeuvre.
The interview’s central argument is that India’s balancing act is not simply equidistance between Washington and Beijing. It is a combination of firm positions, selective cooperation and efforts to preserve choices. Along the China border, that means maintaining deployments while pursuing dialogue. With the US, it means seeking trade and energy gains while recognising that policy can change. For Gupta, the common thread is that India must stand its ground - and keep alternative paths open.
- Shishir Gupta is Executive Editor at Hindustan Times and one of India's top journalists covering national security, strategic affairs, foreign policy and geopolitics.
Over the past three decades, he has extensively reported on India's military, diplomatic and security landscape, covering every major conflict and national security challenge, from the 1999 Kargil War and the 2020 East Ladakh standoff to Operation Sindoor in 2025.
He has also covered major terror attacks, including the IC-814 hijacking, the 26/11 Mumbai attacks and the 2025 Pahalgam terror strike, along with numerous Pakistan-backed terrorist incidents in the Kashmir Valley and across India.
He has reported on national and state elections for more than three decades.
A recognised authority on strategic affairs, Gupta has covered India's nuclear programme since the Pokhran-II (Shakti series) tests in May 1998 and has written extensively on global nuclear issues, Indian diplomacy and the country's expanding global outreach.
He has also reported widely on international conflicts and terrorism, with a special focus on the Indian subcontinent.
Gupta has interviewed Prime Minister Narendra Modi more than four times, including Modi's first interview with the print media after becoming Prime Minister in May 2014.
His other interviews include three with the Dalai Lama, as well as conversations with Benjamin Netanyahu, Amit Shah, Yogi Adityanath, S.
Jaishankar, Nirmala Sitharaman and Piyush Goyal.
He is the author of Indian Mujahideen: The Enemy Within (Hachette, 2011) and Himalayan Face-off: Chinese Assertion and Indian Riposte (Hachette, 2014).
He was awarded the Chevening-Wolfson Joint Scholarship at Wolfson College, University of Cambridge, UK, in 1998 and participated in the International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP) of the US State Department in 2006.
He received the Ben Gurion Prize from Israel in 2011 and the K.
Subrahmanyam Prize for Strategic Studies in 2015 from the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA).
Since 2024, he has hosted Point Blank, Hindustan Times' weekly YouTube show on global geopolitics.

US President Donald Trump has launched a fresh attack on comedian Bill Maher, calling him a “complete and total loser” in a lengthy Truth Social post days after the two had dinner at the White House, an event Trump had initially described as “great”.
The 1,323-word post, which CNN described as Trump's longest-ever social media post based on an analysis, came after Maher mocked the president's approval ratings and made jokes about him during Friday's episode of HBO's 
Real Time with Bill Maher
.
Trump began his Sunday post by attacking Maher and the comedian's show, accusing him of dishonesty and questioning the quality of his programme. He also targeted Chuck LaBella, a longtime business partner of Maher, who previously worked on Trump's reality television show 
The Apprentice
.
“Let's talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” Trump wrote, criticising the comedian's ratings and claiming that HBO had lost the quality and popularity it once enjoyed.
The president later accused Maher of using a “Laughter Machine” to generate audience reactions, arguing that viewers laughed even when the comedian's remarks were not funny.
“Bill Maher lied, but he lies about everything,” Trump wrote, before saying he would no longer watch the programme.
Trump disputes Maher's account of White House dinner
The outburst marked a sharp shift from Trump's public comments following his October 15 dinner with Maher, ESPN host Stephen A. Smith and musician Kid Rock at the White House.
The day after the meeting, Trump had described it as a “great dinner” and said he liked Maher, adding that the comedian liked him more than people realised.
However, the president's tone changed after Maher discussed the meeting on his HBO show. The comedian joked about Trump's approval ratings and said he had spent four hours at the White House without receiving any compliments from the president about his appearance.
Trump disputed the duration of the meeting in his Truth Social post, saying it lasted around two hours or possibly less.
“Overall, I thought it was a good meeting,” Trump wrote, adding that he had learned nothing from the conversation and felt it had been a waste of time.
Trump also claimed that LaBella had repeatedly contacted him to arrange meetings with Maher and had told him that the comedian respected him.
The president recalled their first dinner in March 2025, alleging that Maher had been nervous during the meeting and had appeared with bruising around his eye and nose. Trump also accused the comedian of being dishonest about his views.
Maher, meanwhile, had used Friday's programme to make jokes about Trump's political standing and his comments about men's physiques.
Trump claims record Republican support
Trump also rejected Maher's remarks about his declining approval ratings, claiming 98% to 99% support among Republicans. However, CNN's October 21 poll put his approval rating among Republicans at 74%, a new low in the network's polling. Trump's figures appeared to refer to a separate poll of self-identified MAGA Republicans.
Trump also threatened to have Republicans stop covering Maher, though it was unclear whether he meant Republican guests on the comedian's show or conservative media outlets.
Trump considers moving White House reporters
Trump also confirmed he was considering relocating White House reporters from their longtime workspace to free up space for other uses.
The 1,323-word post surpassed his previous record, a 723-word rant published in May. Factbase, which tracks Trump's social media activity, said it was his longest-ever post across 97,455 posts dating back to 2011.
Trump ended with his familiar sign-off: “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

articles.title: India-China Ties: Beyond the Border - NEWSTRAIL
articles.summary: India-China Ties: Beyond the Border  NEWSTRAIL
articles.full_text:
At the best of times, India’s relations with China have been only delicately calm. It doesn’t take much to pitchfork them into the headlines. One such instance was when Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police Shatrujeet Kapur revealed on Thursday that face-offs were continuing at multiple points along the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh.
The Opposition Congress seized on the comments and accused the government of offering “clean chits” to Beijing when the border was far from calm. The Foreign Ministry promptly clarified that tranquillity along the border is disrupted whenever Chinese forces “diverge from established patrolling patterns”. This confirmed, rather obliquely, what the ITBP chief had said.
Relations had plummeted in June 2020 when the two armies clashed in the Galwan Valley, resulting in the deaths of 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops. Since then, there has been a thaw in ties on both political and economic fronts. Last month, Chinese President Xi Jinping was in India for the BRICS summit. Both Xi and Prime Minister Narendra Modi affirmed that the two countries are “partners rather than rivals”.
After key patrolling and disengagement agreements in Ladakh, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said bilateral ties were “better today than two years ago”. A few weeks ago, Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani said the border situation was stable and there was “no cause for concern”. The economic front, too, has seen a paradoxical upswing, with bilateral trade surging to over $150 billion.
The flipside is that it remains a one-sided business: imports from China stand at $131 billion, while exports to China are only $19 billion. All this indicates a deep structural divergence in how the two nations view each other. While New Delhi maintains that “the state of the border determines the state of the relationship” and peace along the Line of Actual Control is a prerequisite for normal ties, Beijing has pushed for delinking the territorial dispute from diplomatic and economic engagement.
In an era of global interdependence, India can’t afford to allow bilateral relations to be held hostage to border issues. Even while working to resolve the differences regarding the Line of Actual Control and strengthening its military capabilities, India must make every effort to parallelly deepen economic and culturalties.
The government must seek better access to Chinese markets while pursuing sustained domestic self-reliance in order to reduce imports from China. Culturally, both nations should promote student exchanges, academic partnerships, language programmes, direct air connectivity and cultural interactions.

articles.title: Israel votes tomorrow: What’s at stake for India as Bibi faces tough fight - The Economic Times

articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
But as Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, October 27, the result, for India, matters beyond the political fate of “Bibi”, as Netanyahu is popularly known. Defence cooperation, trade negotiations, technology partnerships and India's delicate balancing act between Israel and Iran will all remain important considerations.
Netanyahu's Likud party has lost ground in opinion polls since the Hamas attack, although the contest has narrowed as voting approaches. Neither his coalition nor the opposition has a clear path to the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-member parliament, the Knesset. The result could therefore lead to prolonged coalition negotiations rather than an immediate change of government.
Also Read: Israel election 2026: Netanyahu might be finished but his policies toward the Palestinians will largely endure
For New Delhi, the bigger question is whether a change in Israeli leadership may alter the pace of bilateral cooperation or Israel's approach to a region where India has several competing strategic and economic interests.
India-Israel ties unlikely to change dramatically
India and Israel elevated their relationship to a “Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity” during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Israel in February 2026. The two countries agreed to deepen cooperation in defence, trade, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, semiconductors, agriculture, water management and space.
He said India's relationship with Israel is highly valued and that defence and technology cooperation provide a foundation for continuity. However, a change of leadership could introduce a new dimension to bilateral ties, depending on whether the next prime minister establishes a rapport with Modi.
The distinction matters because the relationship has expanded beyond the personal ties between the two leaders. Agreements covering defence, investment, technology and trade have created institutional links that can support cooperation even if Israel's political leadership changes.
Defence and technology remain central to the partnership
Defence is one of the most important pillars of India-Israel ties. The partnership includes military equipment, research and development, technology sharing and opportunities for joint manufacturing.
The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation on November 4, 2025, to strengthen industrial and technological collaboration. During Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Israel in February 2026, they agreed to deepen cooperation across defence platforms, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and other critical technologies.
Also Read: Israel election 2026: Who is challenging Benjamin Netanyahu for power?
The technology push extends beyond military equipment. Both sides agreed to raise their contributions to the India-Israel Joint Research Calls from $1 million to $1.5 million each, taking the combined contribution to $3 million. They also welcomed a plan to establish an India-Israel Centre of Excellence in Cybersecurity in India.
Semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology, agriculture and water management are among the other areas identified for closer cooperation, according to the joint statement issued during Modi’s visit. The two countries also agreed to deepen collaboration in AI through a dedicated cooperation agreement.
The Tehran factor: India's balancing act between Israel and Iran
The election is taking place against a wider regional backdrop that makes India's diplomatic choices more complicated. New Delhi has strengthened its strategic partnership with Israel while maintaining relations with Iran, which remains important for regional connectivity and India's access to Afghanistan and Central Asia.
The Chabahar port project on Iran's southeastern coast was designed to provide an alternative route to Afghanistan and Central Asia, bypassing Pakistan. India has invested in the development of the port and signed a 10-year contract in May 2024 for the operation of the Shahid Beheshti terminal, as ET Bureau had previously reported.
However, the project faces uncertainty following the expiry of a conditional US sanctions waiver on April 26, 2026. The Indian government has said it remains in touch with relevant stakeholders to address the implications. India has fulfilled its $120 million financial commitment under the port agreement, but the future course of its involvement remains a matter of discussion.
India's engagement with Iran has also continued at the leadership level. Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New Delhi in September 2026, with the two leaders discussing regional developments. Modi stressed the importance of protecting freedom of navigation, international commerce and the safety of seafarers amid the wider conflict.
For India, instability involving Israel and Iran can have consequences well beyond diplomacy. Disruptions to shipping, higher transport and insurance costs, and uncertainty around energy supplies can affect businesses and trade. Any escalation could also complicate connectivity plans and India's economic engagement with the region.
What the Israeli election could mean for regional security
Netanyahu's opponents have criticised his handling of the October 7 Hamas attack, the government's approach to military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews and Israel's growing international isolation, as per reports by AP.
Pollard said the Hamas attack had become a central issue in the election because many Israelis hold Netanyahu responsible for the security failure.
“Netanyahu has been trying to sort of offload that blame onto the security establishment, onto the intelligence establishment, even his political rivals,” he said, according to TOI.
The analyst said Netanyahu had also taken credit for military successes since the attack, leaving voters to decide how they assess his record.
Also Read: Resumption of war with US, Israel won't change Tehran's stance: Iran FM Araghchi
“So the question is, will Israel believe that version or not? And that's going to be quite crucial because a lot of people have been personally burned by this,” Pollard added.
Pollard also pointed to the debate over exemptions from compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews, particularly as reservists face repeated deployments.
“Equal conscription of everybody is a major focus. Those who don't serve shouldn't be able to benefit from the welfare state. But the issue is more about the ultra-Orthodox because they're core members of Netanyahu's coalition,” he said.
Other issues include demands for a national commission of inquiry into the October 7 attack and opposition to Netanyahu's proposed judicial reforms. His far-right coalition partners have also faced criticism over policies towards Palestinians.
Pollard said Netanyahu had presented himself as a leader willing to withstand international pressure, while opponents argued that his coalition had contributed to Israel's growing isolation.
Pollard said a change of government would not bring major changes to Gaza policy, as Israel would not want to return to the security conditions that existed before October 7.
“There was a ceasefire deal with US President Trump, which said that the hostages will be returned. That did happen, and Hamas will disarm. That did not happen. So as far as Israel is concerned, essentially that conflict is not over,” he said.
Trade and investment are another test for India-Israel ties
Beyond defence and security, trade negotiations will be an important measure of whether the partnership continues to deepen.
India and Israel are working towards a proposed free trade agreement, with negotiations covering goods, services, rules of origin, intellectual property and customs procedures. A deal could improve market access and create more opportunities for businesses in both countries.
As of FY26, bilateral merchandise trade between India and Israel stood at US$ 3.93 billion.
India exports products including engineering goods, chemicals, textiles and machinery to Israel, while imports include chemicals, machinery, electronics and other industrial products. The two countries have also established a bilateral investment agreement intended to provide greater certainty and protection for investors.
The next Israeli government will determine how these initiatives progress. For Indian businesses, the priority will be to ensure that political uncertainty does not delay negotiations or cooperation in emerging technologies.
The relationship also has a direct people-to-people dimension with Netanyahu-Modi bonhomie at the heart of it. During Modi's February visit, the two governments discussed employment opportunities for Indian workers in Israel, including construction, caregiving, manufacturing and high-technology sectors. The governments said up to 50,000 additional Indian workers could arrive over five years, while also stressing the need to safeguard their rights and safety.
Whether the political landscape in Jerusalem shifts or stabilises, much will ultimately depend on the next Israeli government’s ability to maintain momentum in the bilateral ties with India amid the broader strategic alignments and realignments across West Asia.

articles.title: Israel elections 2026: What's at stake for Netanyahu? Key challengers, seats needed to win and more - The Times of India
articles.summary: Israel elections 2026: What's at stake for Netanyahu? Key challengers, seats needed to win and more  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Israel is set to vote on Tuesday, marking its first national election since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack, with Prime Minister 
Benjamin Netanyahu
’s leadership, security record and political future at the centre of the campaign.
Voters are weighing his handling of the attack and the conflicts that followed against concerns over military service exemptions, judicial reforms and the rising cost of living.
With Netanyahu facing a challenge from rival parties, the election is expected to test his ability to retain power after years of conflict and political divisions.
However, with no single party expected to win a majority in the 120-member Knesset, the next government will depend on post-election coalition negotiations as much as the vote itself.
What will decide Israel’s election
Israel’s first national election since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership. While the attack and the security failures surrounding it remain central to the campaign, the debate has focused largely on Netanyahu’s accountability, his handling of the aftermath and his leadership rather than Israel’s military conduct in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, which has broad domestic support.
One of the biggest issues is the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from compulsory military service. With Israel facing a shortage of soldiers and reservists repeatedly called up during wars, the exemptions have fuelled resentment among secular Israelis. Netanyahu’s dependence on ultra-Orthodox parties has made the issue particularly contentious, with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, promising to end the exemptions.
Netanyahu’s proposed judicial overhaul, which triggered mass protests in 2023, remains another point of division. Critics see the changes as an attempt to weaken the Supreme Court and undermine democratic institutions, while Netanyahu has defended them as a way to curb judicial power. The economy and the rising cost of living are also concerns, although they have received relatively little attention during the campaign despite many Israelis struggling with affordability.
Leadership is likely to be a decisive factor, with voters weighing Netanyahu’s experience and security record against criticism of his handling of October 7 and the wars that followed.However, neither of the main political blocs is advocating a major shift on the Palestinian question: both are dominated by parties that support Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank and oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state. With no party expected to win an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, the outcome will also depend on which leader can assemble a governing coalition.
Who are the leading candidates?
Benjamin Netanyahu: Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has been in power for much of the period since 2009. His supporters see him as a strong leader capable of defending Israel, but his political standing has been weakened by the security failures surrounding Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack, his corruption trial and an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Gaza, which he denies. His Likud party has faced a decline in opinion polls, though Netanyahu remains a formidable political survivor and is seeking to form a broad national government.
Gadi Eisenkot: The former military chief, 66, leads the centrist Yashar party and has positioned himself as a security-focused alternative to Netanyahu. Having lost his son in combat in Gaza, Eisenkot has highlighted his military background and personal sacrifices. He has also pledged to end the exemptions from compulsory military service enjoyed by ultra-Orthodox men, an issue that has become a major source of public anger.
Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid: Former prime ministers Bennett, 54, and Lapid have joined forces under a new party called Together. Bennett is a former commando and a right-wing politician, while Lapid comes from the centre. Despite their different political backgrounds, the two previously worked together to oust Netanyahu in 2021. Their campaign has focused on national unity and getting Israel back on track after years of conflict and political division.
Avigdor Lieberman:
 The former defence minister, 68, leads the right-wing Israel Our Home party, which draws considerable support from Israel’s ex-Soviet immigrant community. Once a close ally of Netanyahu, Lieberman left his government in 2018, accusing him of being too soft on Palestinian militants in Gaza. He has since become one of the prime minister’s most vocal critics.
Yair Golan: The former general, 64, heads the Democrats, a left-wing party formed from the remnants of Israel’s Labour party and Meretz. Golan was praised for helping rescue people from a site targeted during the October 7 attack.
Key figures backing Netanyahu
Finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, 46, and national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, are prominent far-right allies of Netanyahu. Smotrich has pushed for expanding Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and opposed Palestinian statehood. Ben-Gvir has advocated tougher measures against Palestinian prisoners, capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants and expanded gun ownership for Israelis. Both have also backed the expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza and Israeli resettlement of the enclave.
Netanyahu has also depended on the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism to maintain his governing coalitions. Their demand to preserve exemptions from compulsory military service for many ultra-Orthodox men has become increasingly contentious as Israel faces wartime manpower shortages.
Who could hold the balance of power?
Parties that are not firmly aligned with either major bloc could prove decisive in determining who forms the next government. These include Raam and the Joint List, which represent Israel’s Arab minority, as well as the new right-wing
People of Israel party and the centre-right Reservists party. Their final strength and willingness to join either camp could shape coalition negotiations after the vote.
With no party typically winning a majority outright, forming a coalition of at least 61 lawmakers is key to forming the government
How elections work in Israel
Israel follows a proportional representation system to elect the 120 members of its parliament, the Knesset. Voters choose political parties rather than individual candidates, and seats are distributed according to each party’s share of the national vote. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of the vote to enter parliament.
Since no single party has ever won an outright majority, forming a government typically requires alliances between multiple parties. The leader who can assemble a coalition with the support of at least 61 lawmakers can form the government, giving smaller parties considerable influence over negotiations and policy decisions.
The election comes after a period of political instability between 2019 and 2022, when Israel held repeated elections. Netanyahu’s current Knesset is among the few in the country’s history to have completed its full four-year term.

articles.title: Cyclone Arnab forms over Bay, to cross India on Wednesday as very severe storm - The Daily Star
articles.summary: Cyclone Arnab forms over Bay, to cross India on Wednesday as very severe storm  The Daily Star
articles.full_text:
A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal has intensified into a cyclone named Arnab, which is forecast to strengthen further before crossing India's Andhra Pradesh coast as a very severe cyclonic storm on Wednesday.
At 6:00am today, the cyclone was located 820 kilometres southwest of Chattogram port, 745 kilometres southwest of Cox’s Bazar port, 785 kilometres south of Mongla port and 745 kilometres south of Payra port.
The maximum sustained wind speed within 54 kilometres of the cyclone’s centre is around 62 kilometres per hour, with gusts or squalls reaching up to 88 kilometres per hour.
The Bangladesh Meteorological Department has asked the maritime ports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla and Payra to lower distant warning signal No 1 and hoist distant warning signal No 2.
Fishing boats and trawlers in the North Bay of Bengal have also been advised to remain close to the coast and navigate with caution.
According to the forecast, the cyclone is likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by early Tuesday morning.
It is then expected to move northwestwards and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast of India on Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm.
Meteorologist Abdul Hamid Mia of the BMD told The Daily Star that Cyclone Arnab was not expected to have a significant impact on Bangladesh.
Coastal areas may experience light rain tomorrow and the following day, but the likelihood of heavy rainfall is low, he said.
After the cyclone makes landfall the day after tomorrow, Dhaka and Rajshahi divisions may also experience light rain, he added.
How cyclones are classified
Cyclones are classified into five categories according to their intensity: cyclonic storm, severe cyclonic storm, very severe cyclonic storm, extremely severe cyclonic storm and super cyclonic storm.
Their intensity is measured based on the average maximum sustained wind speed over a three-minute period.
A cyclonic storm has sustained wind speeds of 62 to 88 kilometres per hour. For a severe cyclonic storm, the speed ranges from 89 to 117 kilometres per hour, while a very severe cyclonic storm has winds of 118 to 165 kilometres per hour.
An extremely severe cyclonic storm has sustained winds of 166 to 221 kilometres per hour. A storm with sustained winds of 222 kilometres per hour or more is classified as a super cyclonic storm.
How Arnab got its name
Thirteen countries in the region jointly name cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. They are Bangladesh, India, Iran, the Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen.
The countries are members of the World Meteorological Organisation’s (WMO) regional panel on tropical cyclones. Storms are named sequentially from a list submitted by these countries.
“Arnab” was one of the names on the list that had not yet been used. Bangladesh proposed the name, which means “sea” or “ocean”.
The practice of naming cyclones began in 2000. According to the WMO, naming storms helps avoid confusion, particularly as more than one cyclone can develop in the same region at the same time.

articles.title: India-US Ties Shift Toward Transactional Diplomacy as Iran Conflict Raises Economic Risks - Siliconindia
articles.summary: India-US Ties Shift Toward Transactional Diplomacy as Iran Conflict Raises Economic Risks  Siliconindia
articles.full_text:
India-US relations are increasingly shifting toward transactional diplomacy as the Iran conflict raises economic risks. The changing relationship could affect trade, energy security, supply chains, and strategic cooperation, putting pressure on both countries to balance economic interests with geopolitical priorities amid growing global uncertainty.
	India and the United States are moving into a more transactional phase of their relationship, with trade negotiations, energy security, defense procurement and geopolitical tensions increasingly shaping bilateral engagement. The shift raises questions about the future of the strategic partnership, particularly as Washington’s approach to Iran and its relations with Pakistan complicate New Delhi’s diplomatic calculations.
The latest concerns follow US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India, during which he paid tribute to the victims of the November 26, 2008, Mumbai terrorist attacks at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel. His visit offered a significant reaffirmation of the two countries’ shared position on cross-border terrorism. However, growing differences over trade policy, immigration restrictions and Washington’s regional priorities continue to strain the relationship.
For India, the challenge lies in preserving long-term strategic cooperation while adapting to a US administration that increasingly evaluates international partnerships through commercial interests and immediate policy outcomes. This approach marks a departure from the strategic convergence that has shaped India-US relations over the past 25 years.
Economic engagement nevertheless remains a major pillar of the relationship. Rubio’s meetings with prominent Indian business leaders, including Mukesh Ambani, Gautam Adani and N. Chandrasekaran, highlighted opportunities across energy, infrastructure, defense and technology. Discussions around Venezuelan crude oil and refining capacity in Texas also demonstrated how commercial interests can sustain bilateral engagement despite political disagreements.
India’s refining industry could play a particularly important role in expanding energy cooperation. Greater purchases of US energy supplies could help Washington increase exports while giving New Delhi additional options to diversify its crude oil sourcing. For Indian refiners, access to competitively priced crude remains important for managing input costs, protecting margins and maintaining export competitiveness.
Also Read: MSME Business Confidence Rises Despite Higher Input Costs, Manufacturing Leads: SIDBI
	However, a bilateral trade agreement remains central to improving the business environment. Both countries need greater clarity on US tariffs affecting Indian exports and a credible framework for addressing Washington’s concerns about its trade deficit. Without predictable tariff arrangements, Indian exporters could face uncertainty when making investment, production and market-expansion decisions.
India’s parallel trade negotiations with the European Union and Canada could strengthen its bargaining position. Diversifying export markets would reduce dependence on any single trading partner and give Indian policymakers greater flexibility when negotiating market access, tariff concessions and investment commitments.
Immigration policy presents another challenge. Tighter US visa rules and growing anti-immigration sentiment could affect Indian professionals, technology companies and businesses that depend on cross-border talent mobility. New Delhi must protect the interests of Indian citizens working overseas while recognizing that Indian Americans, as US citizens, operate within America's domestic political and legal framework.
The conflict involving Iran adds another layer of uncertainty. A prolonged escalation could threaten energy infrastructure, maritime routes and submarine communication cables across the region, disrupting oil supplies, logistics networks and international data connectivity. For India, which depends heavily on imported energy, these risks could translate into higher procurement costs, inflationary pressure and increased uncertainty for businesses.
India therefore has an interest in encouraging de-escalation while strengthening its diplomatic engagement with regional and global powers. Greater coordination with Australia and Japan through the Quad could also help New Delhi contribute more actively to regional stability and the evolving international order.
India-US relations continue to offer substantial commercial and strategic opportunities, but their durability will depend on how effectively both governments manage competing interests. For New Delhi, the priority is to secure tangible economic benefits without sacrificing long-term strategic autonomy, while maintaining cooperation on defense, technology, energy security and counterterrorism.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet in Miami, Florida, on December 14 or 15. This planned discussion occurs in the shadow of a recent military confrontation along the disputed border between India and China in Arunachal Pradesh, which has raised questions about the stability of their diplomatic relations.
Following their previous meeting at the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12, there were initial hopes for an easing of tensions. However, Beijing's recent actions have raised concerns. These include affirming its claim over the Shaksgam Valley, which is Indian territory occupied by Pakistan and handed over to China in 1963. Additionally, China proclaimed sovereignty over the entirety of the western segment of the border between the two countries.
The situation escalated with revelations from Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, the outgoing chief of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), regarding ongoing clashes between the Indian and Chinese forces at various locations along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh. Kapoor indicated that China continues to employ a strategy of steady encroachment, often referred to as 'salami-slicing,' which involves making incremental changes to the existing situation on the ground in disputed areas.
Despite these tensions, India's government appears committed to maintaining dialogue with China. A source familiar with New Delhi's diplomatic approach indicated that India is keen to engage with China, especially following the conclusion of a prolonged military standoff in eastern Ladakh that began in October 2024.
The Union Ministry of External Affairs in New Delhi commented on the situation, noting that disruptions occasionally occur when Chinese forces deviate from established patrol routes. Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal mentioned that both nations continue to utilise available diplomatic and military channels to address unresolved issues and to prevent misunderstandings or escalations along the LAC.
Further complicating matters, an anonymous source in New Delhi stated that the longstanding issues highlighted by Kapoor were part of a broader problem that began in 2023. This situation escalated when the Chinese People’s Liberation Army took aggressive steps to block Indian forces from accessing the Shera 5 patrol point near Taksing, situated in the sensitive Asaphila sector along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh.

articles.title: ‘Physically impossible’: Ukraine hits back at Musk over Starlink restrictions, disputes offensive drone s - The Times of India
articles.summary: ‘Physically impossible’: Ukraine hits back at Musk over Starlink restrictions, disputes offensive drone s  The Times of IndiaUkraine says Starshield back to normal, Musk says Kyiv violated terms  ReutersU.S. Allies Race to Escape SpaceX’s Orbit  WSJMusk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored  BBCStarshield | The non-state sovereigns  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian defence technology adviser has challenged 
Elon Musk
’s claim that Ukraine’s military breached Starlink’s terms of service by using the satellite network for offensive drone strikes, prompting 
SpaceX
 to restrict access to the high-speed technology.
According to CNBC news report, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defence technology, disputed Musk’s explanation in a telegram post on Sunday. He argued that existing operational restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine would have made the type of attacks described by the SpaceX chief technically impossible.
Ukrainian officials have previously said the restrictions disrupted military drone operations and weakened the country’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
Musk alleged on Saturday that Ukraine’s military had violated Starlink’s terms of service by using the network for offensive drone strikes intended to kill people. He made the claim in a post on X.
Beskrestnov questioned Musk’s understanding of how the system operates in Ukraine, pointing out that Starlink’s civilian service does not work inside Russian territory. He also said Ukrainian drones using the technology had been subject to speed limits of 70 to 90 kmph (43 to 56 mph) for several months.
“Consequently, it is physically impossible for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Starlink and Starshield services restored
Ukrainian officials said on Saturday that high-speed connectivity through spacex’s starlink and starshield satellite communication systems had been restored. Kyiv had blamed the service disruption for affecting its drone-based air defence capabilities amid repeated Russian aerial attacks.
Starlink is spacex’s commercial satellite internet network, while Starshield is a military-oriented system designed for government and national security applications using technology developed for Starlink.
Before Musk publicly acknowledged restricting the systems, uncertainty surrounded the decision and who had ordered the changes. Musk had earlier suggested in a social media post that the US government was responsible, but US president Donald Trump said he was unaware of the decision.
Ukrainian officials have also said the restrictions were imposed by Starlink or the US without advance warning, catching the country off guard. Musk has not publicly explained why Ukraine was reportedly not notified before the changes took effect.
Musk and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC’s requests for comment.
Ukraine and allies explore alternatives
The disruption has added urgency to efforts by Ukraine and its partners to develop or secure alternative satellite communication networks that would reduce their dependence on foreign providers.
Poland’s deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk discussed his country’s plans in an episode of the podcast influence zone earlier this month. Ukraine has also announced partnerships involving Norway, finland’s telecommunications company nokia and satellite manufacturer ICEYE as part of efforts to develop alternatives.
Other countries are pursuing similar initiatives. The European union is developing IRIS², a satellite constellation intended to strengthen the bloc’s communications infrastructure and strategic autonomy. However, its first launches are not expected until 2029.
Starlink revenue rises amid growing demand
SpaceX’s Starlink business generated $5.25 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.1 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier.
Consumer subscriptions accounted for $3.12 billion of the quarterly revenue, while government and enterprise customers contributed $2.13 billion.
A range of customers, including non-government organisations, the governments of Poland and France, and the US Pentagon, have paid spacex to supply starlink and Starshield equipment and connectivity services for use in Ukraine.

articles.summary: Egyptian parliament authorises military aid for Saudi Arabia  Al JazeeraEgypt approves military support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks escalate  ReutersEgyptian parliament authorizes Sisi to take measures to support Saudi Arabia  Global TimesEgypt Votes to Defend Saudi Arabia, Risking Houthi Fire  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comEgypt authorised to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthis: How Pakistan and Turkey could change the conflict &nbsp...

Egypt’s parliament has authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis intensify.
The House of Representatives, chaired by Speaker Hisham Badawi, approved the mandate in a vote on Monday.
A parliamentary statement members shared with Reuters said el-Sisi had been authorised to “undertake necessary” measures to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself, should Riyadh request assistance.
The move raises the possibility of Egypt becoming more directly involved in a conflict which has consumed the Gulf and the Red Sea in recent weeks. It follows Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s international airport and facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, Aramco, which have disrupted flights and oil exports.
The Houthi armed group that controls Yemen’s capital, Sanaa is fighting the Saudi-led coalition which backs the internationally recognised government.
Fighting has intensified in recent weeks, deepening the humanitarian crisis that has already devastated Yemen.
‘Purely defensive’
Hussein Haridy, a former Egyptian assistant foreign minister, said Cairo’s involvement in the conflict would be limited to defensive action.
“The decision adopted by the Egyptian parliament today, of course, fully authorizes the president, in his capacity as the commander in chief of the armed forces, to take any measures that the situation would warrant in order to provide Saudi Arabia with whatever it would need in order to defend its territory and its infrastructure against any, outside attacks,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The mission, from an Egyptian point of view, is purely defensive in the sense it’s not directed at any party in the region, whether a state or a group. So now it’s a precautionary measure.”
El-Sisi had also said on Wednesday that any Egyptian military action would be limited to protecting Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks on Yemen.
Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo continued to favour a diplomatic settlement after visiting Riyadh on Wednesday.
The vote followed closed-door parliamentary discussions and an earlier postponement of the military aid authorisation for Saudi Arabia, which is one of Egypt’s most important economic partners.
Egypt’s constitution requires approval from two-thirds of legislators before troops can be sent abroad on combat missions.
Egypt also has a direct stake in Red Sea security. Houthi attacks near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the key route to and from the Suez Canal, have disrupted shipping and reduced canal revenue.
Egypt joined a previous Saudi-led campaign in Yemen in 2015, largely helping secure shipping routes with naval forces.
Cairo has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
El-Sisi also met United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in Cairo on Monday to discuss regional tensions and peace efforts.
According to Egypt’s presidency, Guterres praised Cairo’s efforts to prevent escalation in the Gulf and said diplomacy could help address disputes over Iran’s nuclear programme and shipping.
In a post on X on Monday, Guterres urged “maximum restraint”, warning that further fighting could spiral out of control.
